entries.title: Trump Offers $5,000 ‘Dividend’ to Every American Adult if Republicans Win Midterms
entries.summary: The president said the payments would come from the economic successes that Democrats will halt if they take back Congress.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump promised to pay every American adult $5,000 if Republicans keep their majorities in Congress in November’s midterms.

“Here is my promise,” Trump said Wednesday, “if the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them — because of our tremendous economic success, like in history, we've never had anything like what's happening, but because of our tremendous strength and success economically — I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.”

“That alone should win the midterms,” Trump said, speaking at the party’s midterm convention in Dallas. He added the only condition on the payment, which he dubbed the “Trump dividend,” is that Americans must spend that stimulus in the United States.

There are about 245 million adult citizens in America, meaning Trump’s promise would cost more than $1.2 trillion.

Speaking at the novel Republican midterm convention, Trump compared the proposed payments to a company distributing cash to shareholders and credited his economic policies and tariffs with making them possible.

Federal law bars anyone from offering financial compensation to persuade a voter to cast their ballot in favor of or against a particular candidate.

Trump did not specify when the payments would arrive or detail how the program would be funded. He has previously teased a stimulus payment from tariff money.

Wednesday’s proposal came midway through the president’s remarks in Dallas, where he cast November’s midterms as a choice between preserving his agenda and surrendering gains on immigration, taxes and public safety.

There, he urged Republicans to vote as though he was on the ballot.

“If we lose,” Trump warned, “you're going to lose your border, you're going to lose your tax cuts, you're going to lose your safety and security, you're going to lose your wealth.”

He also pledged to show up for some 35 competitive congressional races before November, promising rallies and town halls to help Republican candidates.

“They might be winning by a little, or losing by a little, or tied,” Trump said. “We can win every one of those races, but I’m going to go to every one of those states for congressmen and for senators.”

That effort, he said, would include returning to Texas to campaign for Ken Paxton for Senate.

Trump touted his economic record, celebrated immigration wins, predicted a swift end to the Iran war and called opposition to transgender women in women’s sports “one of our greatest sound bites of all time.”

More than anything, he said, Trump worried Democrats might switch their positions before Election Day: “I’m petrified that they’ll change.”

“The choice in this election is very, very simple. Democrats are asking you to vote for their failed far-left agendas,” Trump said. “And I'm asking you to let us finish the job we began with the greatest two years in the history of the presidency.”

This story has been updated with further comments from President Trump.

entries.title: Fetterman Says He Won’t Leave His Party if Democrats Win the Senate
entries.summary: The Pennsylvania senator’s statement came hours after he made a video cameo at Republicans’ convention.
entries.content:
Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman sought to tamp down speculation about his political future on Wednesday, vowing to remain a Democrat if his party wins the Senate in November.

“I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party-and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on,” Fetterman said in a statement to The Washington Sun.

Fetterman spoke out after his surprise cameo at the Republican convention in Dallas earlier Wednesday night. In a short video appearance, Fetterman criticized democratic socialists and praised his fellow Pennsylvania senator, Republican Dave McCormick. The appearance was highly unusual and drew sharp criticism from some Pennsylvania Democrats.

The senator told The Sun his comments were meant to introduce McCormick “as a great American and friend.”

“We are in different parties, but are both Team PA,” Fetterman said in the statement. “We have delivered hundreds of millions of dollars back to Pennsylvania, fought for improved transportation and affordable housing, and the Steel Way of Life.”

Speculation has grown rampant within both parties about Fetterman’s political future in recent months following his criticism of Democrats while their odds of taking control of the Senate have grown ahead of the November midterms. Some former Fetterman aides have expressed concern he could leave the party in a scenario where Democrats win a Senate majority by a single seat in November, giving him more influence.

Earlier this year, Fetterman said his “red line” for departure would be if the party officially adopts an “anti-Israel” platform. He also set up a joint fundraising committee with McCormick, another highly unusual move that raised eyebrows among his Senate colleagues.

entries.title: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee Loses Democratic Primary
entries.summary: Former CVS executive Helena Foulkes is the first primary challenger to beat a sitting Rhode Island governor in 30 years.
entries.content:
PROVIDENCE, R.I. — Helena Foulkes has defeated Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee in the state’s Democratic primary, ending his bid for a second full term.

McKee’s defeat marks the first time in more than 30 years that a sitting Rhode Island governor has been beaten in a primary. He is the first governor in any U.S. state to lose a party primary since 2018.

Foulkes, a former senior executive at CVS and the retailer Hudson’s Bay, narrowly lost to McKee in a more crowded primary field in 2022, when the governor notably refused to take her concession call.

In their rematch, McKee has been dogged by questions about his administration’s work to replace a critical bridge in the state capital that was abruptly closed due to safety problems in 2023.

Foulkes has leveraged public exasperation over the cost and pace of the bridge project for her argument that McKee's administration isn’t working for most Rhode Islanders.

“People feel like state government just works with a powerful few,” she said. “They don’t think it’s working for them."

McKee, in response, characterized Foulkes as an out-of-touch elite who turned a blind eye to the opioid crisis during her tenure at CVS.

“The option here is somebody who wants to buy this state office who doesn’t have any credibility with their policy thoughts and someone like myself, who has a strong record in terms of working people,” McKee told The Associated Press.

Incumbent governors rarely lose party primaries. The last time it happened in Rhode Island was in 1994, when Democrat Bruce Sundlun lost to state Sen. Myrth York, ending his bid for a third term. In that race, Sundlun was facing multiple controversies and voter fatigue while York ran on reform.

McKee has been governor since 2021, when he stepped into the position after then-Gov. Gina Raimondo was tapped as U.S. commerce secretary.

In 2023, McKee closed the Washington Bridge, a vital link that carries Interstate 195 over the Seekonk River and connects Providence to its eastern suburbs, the south coast of Massachusetts. During the summer, it also carries traffic bound for Cape Cod.

State transportation officials had flagged a “critical failure” in an older part of the bridge, but demolishing and replacing it has taken longer than the governor initially estimated. Traffic continues to flow but has been squeezed into fewer lanes on a newer part of the span. This has led to lengthy commute times for many who cross the bridge daily as signs posted along the bridge thank drivers for their patience.

McKee maintains that his decisions kept people safe and that the bridge construction will be finished by 2028. He often points to Maryland, saying the Washington Bridge will be complete ahead of the replacement of Baltimore's much larger Francis Scott Key Bridge, which collapsed and killed six construction workers in 2024 after a container ship crashed into it.

Foulkes' grandfather and uncle, Thomas and Chris Dodd, were both Democratic U.S. senators in Connecticut. She worked at CVS for 25 years, eventually becoming president of the company’s pharmacy division between 2014 and 2018. She then became chief executive officer of the Canadian retail giant Hudson’s Bay Company before leaving that job in 2020.

When pressed on her time at CVS, Foulkes argued that CVS reduced its opioid dispensing by 40% when she was president of CVS’ pharmacy division. In 2022, after Foulkes had left CVS, the company agreed to pay $5 billion to settle lawsuits nationwide over the toll of opioids without admitting wrongdoing.

The last governor to lose in a primary was former Kansas Gov. Jeff Colyer, who narrowly lost the Republican nomination to Kris Kobach in 2018.

In the Republican gubernatorial primary, Aaron Guckian and Elaine Pelino are vying for the nomination. Guckian is a state trade association executive and was the nominee for lieutenant governor in 2022. He won the two-way primary that year with about 68% of the vote. Pelino is a former actor and first-time candidate. The state party has endorsed Guckian.

Notably, Rhode Island’s primary elections are being held on a Wednesday after state lawmakers moved the date from its typical Tuesday election day because it fell too close to Labor Day.

Only four states hold their primary elections in September: Rhode Island, Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Delaware, which has the latest primary date in the U.S., taking place this year on Sept. 15.

entries.title: Collins Needs to Defy Political Gravity Again — and Trump Isn't Helping
entries.summary: A Canada trade war, an ICE shooting and Iran. How much more can Susan Collins take from Trump and still win?
entries.content:
BATH, Maine — The sun has just emerged from over the Kennebec River, and Republican Sen. Susan Collins is ready to greet workers ahead of the first shift at Bath Iron Works.

Shipbuilders, machinists and welders arrive in fits and starts ahead of the 7 a.m. whistle. Collins and roughly a dozen supporters and campaign staff have one goal: for these union workers to gobble up boxes of T-shirts. The navy blue tees feature “SUSAN” on the pocket (the “USA” in red, white and blue, of course) and “BATH BUILT IS BEST BUILT” displayed around the silhouette of a Navy destroyer.

“T-shirts! Get your T-shirts here!” one staffer yells as workers approach, doing his best impression of a hot dog vendor at a minor league baseball game.

The moment is important for Collins’ team, who confide before the predawn event that it’s a test of sorts. If workers take the shirts? A good sign of where the senator is two months out from Mainers deciding whether to hand her a sixth term in office. And if they don’t? An ominous sign of her prospects.

Luckily for them, medium and 2XL shirts are gone with time to spare before work starts. Even those not taking the shirts are polite enough, telling staffers, “Thanks, I’m all set,” or a straight up “No, thank you,” with minimal hostilities.
Susan_Collins_Bath_09012026_16 copy.jpg (5541x3694, AR: 1.50)There’s a reason the crew was very familiar with Collins. She’s helped steer billions of dollars and years of Pentagon contracts to the shipyard, which is the state’s fourth-largest employer. Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee, has widespread union support, but Collins retains some loyalty among working-class voters.

Collins Argues Her Senate Seniority Translates Into Millions for Maine

It’s part of yet another all-politics-is-local strategy that Collins, the Senate Appropriations Committee chair, is banking on to lock down another term. Check out a sampling of her ads or campaign appearances and the message is clear: She’s responsible for securing money to rebuild a fire station or other local projects that generate jobs. That constituent services work is what Democrats concede is formidable.

“It’s given me a once-in-a-century opportunity to really deliver for the people of Maine. … I have delivered for small communities all across the state,” Collins told The Washington Sun in an interview, noting that 45 new and rebuilt fire stations exist due to federal money she’s brought home. “That matters.”

Despite that pitch, Collins finds herself in yet another reelection dogfight where she’s working to defy political gravity.

She’s the lone Senate Republican representing a state carried by former Vice President Kamala Harris two years ago. But increasingly it’s the impact of President Donald Trump’s policies that is causing her constituents to consider electing a Democrat.

Trump’s Immigration and Trade Policies Cause Headaches 

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot and killed a Colombian national in Biddeford, Maine, less than two months ago amid a surge of operations in nearby Portland. But the individual wasn’t the target of the ICE operation, and the fallout has rippled across the state.

More recently, trade negotiations with Canada went belly-up, leading to a nasty break in a longstanding relationship. Collins has pleaded with the administration to resume negotiations, as her state shares a 611-mile border with the neighbor to the north and exported $1.3 billion worth of goods to Canada last year —- 41% of the state’s exports. Instead, the president is posting memes about the Canadian prime minister.

“It is [a lot]. It’s certainly not helpful. There’s no doubt about that,” Collins told The Sun, adding that voters are “perplexed” and “more puzzled than anything” about the Canada trade war.

According to a Fox News poll taken in early August, 59% of voters in the state view Trump unfavorably — and that was before the trade spat.

It’s also not an accident that Collins is trying to put more distance between herself and the president. During an event in Biddeford, Collins called on ICE to enact more reforms beyond the recent equipping of agents with body cameras. She argued the agency should stop making arrests at “sensitive” locales, including schools, hospitals, doctors offices and places of worship.

She also criticized the president’s lack of strategy for launching a war with Iran, which has reached a seventh month and has grown deeply unpopular with Americans.
Pete Hegseth (4987x3325, AR: 1.50)“The president clearly did not have a well-thought-out plan for how to deal with Iran. To me, it was utterly predictable that Iran would close the Strait of Hormuz,” she told reporters. “That should not have come as a surprise, and the administration and the Department of Defense should have been prepared for that.”

Gas prices in the state are averaging more than $4 per gallon. Mainers are also bracing for rising heating oil costs in the coming months, an issue that could crop up closer to Election Day.

The series of events has Collins’ allies wondering how much more of this she can handle and still win. One source close to the longtime senator noted that of all the potential administration-induced impediments that could crop up, a second ICE shooting is the one that worries them the most and could be too difficult to overcome.

“It’s frustrating. It’s almost exhausting,” Jason Levesque, the former Republican mayor of Auburn, Maine, and a political commentator, said of the string of happenings.

Collins has never been a favorite of the president, and the feeling is mutual.

He said in June that she is “not my best friend at all,” all the while touting her vote streak even though “sometimes she voted against me.” While Trump has indicated support for her, there is a gulf between the two, as they don’t have much of a relationship.

“They don’t interact often,” the source close to Collins said, noting that they have cordial interactions when they see each other at White House events.

“She’s not calling him about policy stuff, and he’s not calling her either,” the source added.

Instead, her preferred point of contact in the administration is Vice President JD Vance, who she became friendly with during his brief senatorial tenure.
Vance (2884x1923, AR: 1.50)Vance recently told supporters during a late-August event in the state that Collins has been to the Naval Observatory at least a half-dozen times, yet is “the most independent member” of the Senate and “sometimes makes my job just a little bit harder.”

There’s a different type of independence that will be a factor in November. For the first time during the Trump era, Collins will be running without the president on the ballot.

Although the two are like oil and water politically, they complimented each other well across the state in 2020, with Trump giving Collins a boost in rural areas while she overperformed him along the coast. She toppled Sara Gideon, her Democratic opponent, by 8.5 percentage points and cleared 50%, bypassing the state’s ranked choice system entirely.

This go-round, Collins has sought to beef up her support with some of Trump’s most ardent backers. She repaired what was once a fraught relationship with former Republican Maine Gov. Paul LePage, the favorite to succeed Rep. Jared Golden in the 2nd Congressional District.

She’s relying on her record controlling federal spending bills, including what she has procured for rural areas. Collins has touted that she secured more than $428 million in earmarks for the state. She also has the financial muscle to get that message out after being drowned out by Democratic spending in 2020.

“I know the people of rural Maine. I am one of the people of rural Maine,” she said. “I think people understand authenticity and that they also appreciate how hard I work for rural Maine.”

Collins admits the race against Jackson, the former state Senate president who only entered the race after Graham Platner’s swift exit stage left after being accused of sexual assault, is not the race she expected.

“We had to start all over again,” Collins said. “This is the strangest race I’ve ever seen.”

Democrats Work to Nationalize the Race After Platner’s Messy Exit 

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has maintained a defiant face about the race, repeatedly declaring that this is the year the party topples Collins. Democrats note that Collins’ approval rating has never been lower and that she votes with Trump at a healthy clip. And they stress that Collins’ vote to confirm Trump’s Supreme Court nominees helped put a stake in Roe v. Wade.

But Democrats in the state remain less sure this strategy will work.

One Maine-based Democratic operative argued that the path for Democrats centers around nationalizing the race and keeping Jackson as generic of a candidate as possible, something Republicans are quickly trying to change. Outside groups — and even Collins herself — have pointed to Jackson’s having two children with his longtime partner, who is his second cousin.

“If Democrats and Troy can keep this race about Donald Trump, affordability and what Susan Collins has or hasn’t done to help with those things, put a check on those things, then Troy has a path to victory, even though it is hard,” the operative said.
Troy_Jackson_Lewiston_09012026_26 copy.jpg (5600x3733, AR: 1.50)“The challenge is if this race becomes about Susan Collins versus Troy Jackson or anybody else,” they continued. “Susan Collins versus a specific person is really hard because Susan Collins is not a bad politician.”

Even Jackson’s most ardent supporters acknowledge that overcoming Collins’ long-standing ties is a high hurdle.

“I think he’s got a very challenging road ahead,” Portland’s Democratic mayor, Mark Dion, who was among those introducing Jackson at his first town hall in Lewiston, told The Sun in an interview.

The party is still picking up the pieces after Platner’s implosion in July, which forced party activists to choose a replacement that some voters are still smarting over. During his Lewiston town hall, a self-described independent who votes Democratic pressed Jackson, pointing to advertisements that “keep referring to ‘our movement’ that ‘we built.’”

“It feels disingenuous because the movement that was building was built by someone else,” said Tori Leigh. “You weren’t elected by the voters.”

“You are right. I didn’t build this movement. I’ve been saying that all along,” Jackson responded. “This isn’t about Troy Jackson. But I don’t even think this is about Graham. I think it’s about people across this state that know there’s something fundamentally wrong with the way things are going.”

Jackson peppered the rally with criticisms of Collins, arguing that she has lost touch with the state — citing her decision against holding town hall meetings. The pair recently agreed to four debates, with the first one set for Oct. 6.

The biggest roar at the town hall came when Jackson pressed that ICE should be “eliminated.”

There are also fears of an enthusiasm gap on the left.

Multiple attendees at the Lewiston event were quick to note that Platner held a standing room only event at the same location last fall that also featured a place for an overflow crowd. The Jackson event, meanwhile, featured dozens of empty seats in the back of the room.
Troy_Jackson_Lewiston_09012026_04 copy.jpg (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)The Maine-based Democratic operative argued that while state Democrats have reasons for excitement now, that’s “mostly fueled by being mad at Collins, not excited for Troy.”

Other top Democrats conceded that the winds have shifted since the Platner exodus.

“He’s not a pop star. He’d be the first one to tell you that,” Dion said of Jackson, adding that he is more than willing to trade “pop star status for competency.”

Polling since Jackson’s entrance has been limited, with a pair of surveys taken since the start of August showing him in a lead within the margin of error. Operatives from both parties are quick to note that the state is notoriously hard to poll.

Another question surrounding Jackson is whether he can win over enough independents and Democrats who’ve backed Collins over the years. If the Lewiston event is any indication, he has some work to do.

Tom Soule, a Democrat and a retired school principal from nearby Bowdoinham, noted that he’s supported Collins throughout the years but is considering supporting Jackson in order to more effectively take on Trump. He wasn’t a fan of Platner’s but showed up to check out Jackson’s pitch.

But Jackson’s inability to explain how he would enact change rather than tick through his positions on issues frustrated him.

He ended up leaving the event early, telling The Sun on his way out: “Not impressed.”

entries.title: D.C.’s To-Do List for Janeese Lewis George Keeps Getting Longer
entries.summary: The presumptive mayor-elect has asked D.C. voters to be “brutally honest.” Now comes the hard part.
entries.content:
In the warm, crowded basement of East Washington Heights Baptist Church, Timothy Harrison sat over a plate of soul food, waiting for his opening.

A Ward 7 resident who helps small businesses get off the ground, Harrison didn’t come to point out everything wrong with D.C. He came with a pitch — and a simple philosophy.

“I don’t complain. I want to help her fix this,” Harrison said, gesturing across a room where neighbors were busy scribbling their hopes and frustrations on colored sticky notes. “Anyone can come in with a complaint. But this is the first part of something. That’s why she deserves the right to work.”

Harrison hoped to pitch D.C.’s presumptive next mayor, Council member Janeese Lewis George, on addressing the root trauma of poverty through street-level mental health teams. It was the kind of deep, neighborhood-level dialogue Lewis George built her council career on. She paused by his row to listen, but with hundreds of other residents waiting to get her attention, the physical scale of her new mandate quickly closed in.

“Mayor, we’re running behind,” a staff member interrupted, whisking her away.

By imploring residents to be “unabashedly honest,” Lewis George has opened the floodgates to a city eager to be heard. From working-class residents east of the Anacostia River pleading for basic sanitation to progressive strongholds in Ward 1 demanding she abolish the police department, the first week of her citywide listening tour laid bare the sheer weight of her incoming transition.
_MG_0068 copy.jpg (5909x3940, AR: 1.50)With a clear path to victory awaiting her in November as the Democratic nominee for D.C. mayor, Lewis George has said she is using this in-between period to hunt for low-hanging fruit — policy shifts that don’t require massive budget fights and can also immediately prove to voters that her vision of government works.

But taking in thousands of granular demands also creates the opportunity for immense political friction, as the incoming administration must determine a way to meet voters’ expectations without collapsing beneath them.

It’s a tightrope she acknowledges openly.

“Everything y’all put on this list — the micro and macro things — we’re going to take a check and say, ‘Hey, did you do what you said you were going to do?’” she told the crowd. “We’re basically creating accountability for myself.”

A paper trail of promises

Accountability in government carries a unique and historic burden for residents like Joel Crooms. The 73-year-old says he embodies the wary optimism of a generation that remembers the tangible community investments of past leaders like “mayor for life” Marion Barry — those Crooms felt focused on direct neighborhood needs rather than corporate interests.

He compared Lewis George with the outgoing mayor, Muriel Bowser, whom he accused of prioritizing real estate developers over everyday residents. For Crooms, a resident of Ward 7, Lewis George’s success hinges on breaking that mold.

“As long as she doesn’t sell us out and turn into Bowser in two years,” Crooms said. “But you never know. Money talks.”

At Ward 8’s meeting, 18-year-old Atrayu Lee offered a different kind of generational mandate. A campaign volunteer whose political awakening began by publicly calling out city lawmakers for neglecting youth, the American University freshman challenged the city’s reliance on traditional policing to reduce crime. He implored D.C. leaders to instead make the city’s summer youth-employment program — named after Barry — a year-round affair.

He also urged lawmakers to find a way to get more mental health counselors in D.C. public schools, where he noted supply has failed to meet demand — a hurdle he faced recently as a student at Thurgood Marshall Academy.

“Instead of punishing people for circumstances that may be out of their control, let’s help them and uplift them,” Lee said.
_MG_9892 copy.jpg (5335x3557, AR: 1.50)_MG_9853 copy.jpg (7200x3445, AR: 2.09)Yet the most volatile pressure tests for Lewis George’s progressive platform are surfacing in liberal strongholds like Ward 1, where she captured a commanding 66% of the primary vote. Inside her listening session at All Souls Unitarian Church in Columbia Heights, a friendly reception came paired with sky-high expectations.

Attendees pressed her on a sprawling docket: neighborhood trauma tied to the police department’s past collaborations with ICE; chronic battles over developer-driven displacement; and yawning equity gaps in neighborhood public schools.

The sheer volume of those expectations was visible at every stop on the tour, where residents have been encouraged to write their ideas on sticky notes and place them on oversize poster boards under headers like “Clean Up Trash Here!” and “Other Ideas You Have For Helping Your Community.”

Within hours, bright neon squares would crowd out the printed margin, creating a paper trail of demands calling for everything from 24-hour daycare to traffic-calming speed cameras.

For the thousands of residents who couldn’t cram into the overflowing listening sessions last week, the campaign rolled out an online “people’s survey” to capture even more data, making the solicitation of resident ideas a round-the-clock effort.

Back in Ward 7, Donna Morrow was eager to add to the paper trail. While most attendees staked out a single grievance per sticky note, she filled a bright purple square until her list of neighborhood repairs ran so long it spilled onto a second one.

“I’m gonna start writing them down at home as I think of them,” Morrow said. “Then I’ll call her office.”

From listening to governing 

For Lewis George and her transition team, the citywide tour is designed to function as something of a stress test for her own platform. As her campaign apparatus converts into a governing machine, she’s conceded that the flood of feedback has already forced her to look past her usual legislative playbook.

After hearing an unexpectedly high volume of concerns regarding health care access and provider rollbacks, for example, Lewis George said she directed her team to pivot and more carefully consider how to incorporate the feedback into her administration’s early plans.
_MG_9993 copy.jpg (5219x3479, AR: 1.50)“That’s the difference between legislating and governing,” Lewis George told reporters after the Ward 1 session. “Governing requires me to now take into account some things that maybe I felt personally as a council member. I’m going into these [meetings] open to my mind being changed.”

Lewis George said she’d demonstrate her flexibility well before she’s sworn in. When she returns to the council following summer recess later this month, she intends to put forward legislation aimed at meeting the most urgent constituent demands, setting the stage for immediate executive action when she takes office.

Still, critics and allies alike are watching closely to see if her populist vision can survive the realities of municipal budgeting and other frictions that come with executive power.

The immediate test, Ward 1 Democratic Council nominee Aparna Raj noted, will be how she balances quick administrative wins — like easing small business permits — against the massive, multiyear battles that would likely accompany landmark proposals like social housing or universal child care.

Lewis George insists this pressure is precisely what should drive her administration. Standing among the lingering crowd as another listening session drew to a close, she embraced the challenges ahead.

“I’m less worried about disappointing people and more excited about surprising people,” she said.

Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 10, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

Today’s Daily Digit — 4/10: Feeling like August with highs around 90 and humidity pushing the heat index toward the mid-90s. Scattered storms possible late. Full forecast from Capital Weather.



THE LATEST

What happens when D.C.’s presumptive next mayor asks the entire city to be “unabashedly honest” about what it needs? She gets a massive, complicated to-do list.

Janeese Lewis George is spending the months before November’s general election on a citywide listening tour. From residents east of the Anacostia River pleading for consistent sanitation services, to progressives in Ward 1 demanding she abolish the police department, the tour has so far laid bare the sheer weight of Lewis George’s coming mandate, The Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler reports.

“Everything y’all put on this list — the micro and macro things — we’re going to take a check and say, ‘Hey, did you do what you said you were going to do?’” Lewis George told the large crowd gathered for Ward 7’s listening session. “We’re basically creating accountability for ourselves.”

But taking in thousands of demands creates immense political friction. As her campaign converts into a governing machine, Lewis George must figure out how to meet voters’ sky-high expectations. She concedes that the flood of feedback is already forcing her to look past her usual legislative playbook, particularly after hearing an unexpected number of concerns regarding health care access citywide.

“That’s the difference between legislating and governing,” Lewis George said. “Governing requires me to now take into account some things that maybe I felt personally as a council member.”

Observers say the immediate test will be how she balances quick administrative wins — like easing small-business permits — against the massive, multiyear battles that would probably accompany landmark proposals such as social housing or universal child care.

“I’m less worried about disappointing people and more excited about surprising people,” she said.

_MG_0068 copy.jpg (5909x3940, AR: 1.50)



DEEP DIVE

The level of cannabis competition in the D.C. region is about to get much higher.

With Virginia set to roll out recreational sales next July, cannabis retailers in D.C. are getting increasingly nervous that they won’t survive, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports. That’s because Virginians have long made the drive into D.C. for their cannabis needs, accounting for a significant amount of what vendors in the city are selling.

“Virginia coming online will definitely, probably take 20% to 25% of our business,” said Johannes Cassidy-Seyoum, the owner of High Demand in Capitol Hill. “A good amount of our customers come from Richmond, Fredericksburg. They make a trip maybe two, three times a month and they stock up.”

Of the 2,101 non-D.C. residents who patronized D.C. cannabis retailers in July, 807 came from Virginia, according to the city’s Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Administration.

On top of high rents, cannabis sellers in D.C. face an obstacle Virginia doesn’t: Capitol Hill. For more than a decade, Congress has prohibited D.C. from legalizing recreational sales. As a workaround, D.C. has expanded its medical cannabis program, allowing anyone — including Virginians — to self-certify. But that adds paperwork and fees.

“We have a lot more restrictions in D.C. right now than Virginia will next year,” said Caroline Crandall, who owns Green Theory in the Palisades, a short drive from Virginia. “[We’re trying to] figure out ways to remain competitive.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

Metro is debuting a systemwide redesign of its station signage, to mixed reviews. Exits will no longer be labeled by the street intersections they lead to, but rather a letter that corresponds to attractions near each exit, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. Graphics showing the remaining stops on each line will be taken off the wall of each terminal, relegating full route information to signs on the platform.

Riders pushed back on social media, saying the new signs are less intuitive and make information harder to find, but Metro defended the effort. “It may seem unfamiliar at first glance, but multiple rounds of feedback were considered to finalize this effort,” WMATA said in a post.

A National Guard member deployed in D.C. is facing felony charges after being accused of pointing a loaded service weapon at a fellow soldier during an argument over Army grooming standards, The Sun’s Jenna Monnin reports.

The candidate list for D.C.’s 345 Advisory Neighborhood Commission seats is nownullfinal. And if you were hoping for a competitive, hyperlocal election in your neighborhood come November, you may need to lower expectations. According to the D.C. Board of Elections, 82% of the ANC seats have either no candidate or a single person on the ballot for the general election, leaving a mere 62 contested ANC races citywide.

A TPS reprieve, but for how long? The Department of Homeland Security hasn’t yet decided whether it will terminate the Temporary Protected Status held by 200,000 Salvadorans across the U.S., The Sun’s Manuela Silva reports. That status — which protects them from deportation — has been extended for decades, largely due to political conflict and natural disasters in the Central American country. There are an estimated 30,000 Salvadorans with TPS in the Washington region.





FROM VIRGINIA

DSC05422.JPG (3504x2336, AR: 1.50)
Flock off. Several elected officials in Alexandria are pushing the city’s police department to end its contract with Flock, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. The automatic license-plate readers have been credited with helping police solve high-profile crimes, but they have also prompted concerns over privacy and surveillance. There are 61 Flock cameras in Alexandria. Some activists in D.C. have raised their own concerns with the city’s 67 Flock cameras.





TALK TO TOM

Tom Sietsema is back answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here.

With the season about to change, I want to plan a road trip. Where would you go for a dining escape within a few hours of D.C.? 

In the exurbs of Virginia, I’m high on Three Blacksmiths in Sperryville. The drill is a single seating for up to 20 guests in a handsome dining room, and a seasonal, five-course menu prepared by chefs who double as your attendants by introducing the dishes to you. Then there’s Maude & the Bear in Staunton, which began life as a Montgomery Ward home kit more than a century ago, helmed by chef Ian Boden. He, too, offers a five-course list — along with nine- and 22-course tasting menus — that the chef says includes “several little surprises.”

In Maryland, I’m always happy to settle into the inviting, Old World interior at Bas Rouge in historic Easton. Its details are rich: Zalto stemware, Bernardaud china and an antique Lobmeyr crystal chandelier to illuminate the space. As for the cooking, Harley Peet won the Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic award from the James Beard Foundation two years ago.

In the full Q&A: Corkage fees, cramped dining rooms and thoughts on Rye Bunny. 





SPORTS

Want proof that the Nats have truly entered a new era? Look at their minor league teams. The Sun’s Dave Sheinin reports that Washington’s new regime has overhauled the farm system with advanced analytics, new technology and a new philosophy.

“For us, it’s: ‘Let’s tether ourselves to what the evidence says contributes to winning and do our best to actually help our people get there,’” Nats president Paul Toboni told The Sun. Up in the majors, the Nats have made a habit of blowing saves this year. In fact, Washington has already set an MLB record with 38 blown saves this season. But The Sun’s Jesse Dougherty writes that the numbers are not as bleak as they appear.

After a near-perfect rookie season, Jayden Daniels had a rough 2025. Dealing with injuries, he missed more games than he played as Washington stumbled to a 5-12 record. Now, Daniels is looking to put all of that — the good and the bad — behind him. The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson reports that Washington’s quarterback has learned a new playbook, brushed off criticism and even added some muscle as he prepares for Year 3.

Washington Spirit star Trinity Rodman was busy Wednesday morning. After watching boyfriend Ben Shelton battle Carlos Alcaraz late into the night at the U.S. Open, she made her way from New York to D.C. for practice. Shelton finished off his five-set win around 3:30 a.m. and, according to the Spirit, Rodman showed up to train by 9:30.

entries.title: ‘It’s Trumpapalooza’
entries.content:
Today’s notice: A cool video reminder that we’re The Washington Sun now. Live from Dallas. The effort to defeat Susan Collins is having a bumpy takeoff. The likely next mayor of D.C. cranks up expectations. Hospitals are ignoring Trump’s pricing transparency rules. And: The Democratic generation gap goes Hollywood.





THE LATEST

Day 1 of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas was most notable for the Democrat who spoke via video and Donald Trump promising a $5,000 payment to every American if Republicans win in November. Sen. Tim Scott (R-South Carolina) said many of the Democrats running for Senate are “dangerous, radical and frankly weird.” A mention of Senate Majority Leader John Thune brought boos. Attorney General Todd Blanche broke Justice Department tradition by giving a speech at the political event — and was received well by the crowd.

But who is the crowd? This is a strange event at a strange time. Polls and historic headwinds suggest Republicans are wasting valuable general election time rallying around the president. And yet: “It’s Trumpapalooza,” Ty Bommarito, part of a conservative cadre from Michigan State University invited to sit on the floor, told The Sun’s Jasmine Wright. “It’s to get everyone excited for the midterms, and I think it will energize the base.”

But for the most part, it’s not young people in the audience. “I think what you find, there’s a lot of people who have been delegates or alternate delegates in the past that are here today,” Pennsylvania state Sen. Scott Martin told The Sun’s Oriana González. “People who come here are paying their way, you know, on their flight costs, on their hotel — it’s not a freebie for them.”

They’re in Dallas for Trump, or at least his vision of Republican politics.

About that Democrat we mentioned, Sen. John Fetterman appeared in a video message to the crowd. In theory, it was an introduction to his Pennsylvania colleague, Republican Sen. Dave McCormick, whom Fetterman has regularly made public appearances with. But there was an undertone aimed at some in the Democratic Party: “I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life,” Fetterman said.

So is this guy going to switch parties, or what? “I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party-and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on,” Fetterman said in a statement to The Sun. Keep a close eye on that should the Senate flip part.

FROM THE GREAT AI FREAKOUT


Doomscrolling has a whole new meaning: This week, a couple of AI researchers connected to the two biggest American AI companies revealed in a public online conversation that some in the industry are busily working away on a technology they believe could kill all humans.

“Anytime you have folks talking about AI moving towards extinction of human life, I think that’s got to rise to the top of priorities for us in Congress,” Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on House Oversight, told The Sun. He promised to investigate AI companies if Democrats win the majority. Hey, Claude: Will that be too late?

Others who have been AI skeptics all along, like Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), are taking this opportunity for an I told you so. Sanders is hosting a private briefing for senators with industry experts next week to discuss the “extraordinary dangers that AI poses for humanity.”

In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate, told The Sun’s Igor Bobic that it’s time for a pause on all AI development. “The speed at which this is all progressing is really quite alarming,” he said.

FROM MAINE


Democrats still haunted by the primary? “I think he’s got a very challenging road ahead,” Mark Dion, the Democratic mayor of Portland, Maine, said of his party’s nominee for Senate, Troy Jackson. The Sun’s Al Weaver has a deep dive into the Maine race as it enters the general election — and finds incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins activating her traditional all-politics-is-local strategy while Jackson struggles to unite a base fractured by the rise and dramatic fall of Graham Platner.

Al reports that one person who attended a town hall with Jackson criticized him because the movement he’s trying to harness “was built by someone else,” meaning Platner. Democrats hope this race will center around Trump and the economy, not Collins and Jackson as candidates. Republicans want the opposite — and Collins is putting a lot of emphasis on her distance from the president and his actions (read: Canadian tariffs).

“It’s certainly not helpful. There’s no doubt about that,” Collins told The Sun, adding that voters are “perplexed” and “more puzzled than anything” about the Canada trade war.

FROM THE DISTRICT


Can Janeese Lewis George meet expectations? The populist lefty presumptive next mayor of D.C. has asked residents to tell her what they want — and they are definitely doing that, The Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler reports. On the road with Lewis George, Michael clocked a paper trail of demands calling for everything from universal child care to traffic-calming speed cameras. That’s not counting the online requests, and she’s not even mayor yet.

More: How Virginia Could Smoke Out D.C.’s Cannabis Industry • Alexandria Leaders Want to Get Rid of the City’s Flock Cameras





THE BIG ONE

Hollywood leaves Democrats to their civil war: Screenwriter Gregg Hurwitz was one of several storytellers who actively helped hone the Democratic Party’s 2018 winning message. He says this of 2026: “The Democratic Party right now is torn in a couple directions, and some of those directions I’m no longer willing to work for or countenance, and so I’m a lot more sparing about it.”

The contours of this are familiar. Hurwitz and the other messaging gurus from Tinseltown who helped in 2018 are among those turned off by the rise of the ultraleft and the party’s growing generation gap. The Sun’s Oriana González and Kadia Goba report on a far-flung front of the intraparty debate.

It’s another sign of what’s to come for a potential Speaker Hakeem Jeffries. He helped spearhead his party’s work with Hollywood as co-chair of the House Democrats’ messaging arm in 2018. Jeffries’ staff met with screenwriters to talk campaign messaging as recently as this July, The Sun has found.

But he may not like what they have to say these days. “Only Democrats have a hard time with this, and that’s because we tend to speak in these cotton candy terms that sound like they were dreamed up in the Harvard faculty lounge,” one filmmaker who still works with Democratic candidates said.





PODCAST

From your favorite podcast app: Today, Sun Managing Editor Kate Nocera chats with reporter Igor Bobic about our name change. Then, Igor is joined by congressional reporters Al Weaver and Avani Kalra for a look into Trump’s new ads in battleground states and how data centers are shaping midterm races.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Hospitals are not following Trump’s pricing transparency rules for the most part, The Sun’s Paige Winfield Cunningham reports. Fewer than one in five hospitals owned by the nation’s largest health systems are displaying dollar amounts for at least half of their posted items and services, despite rules written during the first Trump administration requiring them to do so. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz has said he’ll crack down on noncompliance.

entries.title: Most U.S. Hospitals Aren’t Posting Their Prices Despite Trump’s Rules
entries.summary: The Trump administration has threatened a crackdown after five years of hospitals skirting the rules.
entries.content:
Most hospitals still aren’t posting how much they charge for medical services, five years into federal transparency rules that require them to do so.

Fewer than one in five hospitals owned by the nation’s largest health systems are displaying dollar amounts for at least half of their posted items and services, according to a survey of 2,000 hospitals by price transparency group PatientRightsAdvocate.org provided to The Washington Sun.

“This is law for us to know prices,” said Cynthia Fisher, the group’s founder. “It is not hard.”

The Trump administration has demanded hospitals start complying with the transparency regulation. The rule was written by the first Trump administration and went into effect in 2021 as part of an effort to eliminate the opaque pricing schemes that leave patients ignorant of what they’ll have to pay for a visit or procedure.

In April, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services sent warning letters to more than 500 hospitals and asked some to send compliance action plans. A CMS spokesperson didn’t say whether the agency had enacted any fines yet.

“CMS will continue working to undo four years of bad policy,” the spokesperson said, referring to a regulation update under the Biden administration which gave hospitals some wider latitude. “We’ve sent a clear message to noncompliant hospitals: post your prices or pay the penalty.”

The federal government can fine hospitals as much as $2 million annually for noncompliance. The Biden administration fined about two dozen hospitals. The Trump administration has fined a handful since President Donald Trump took office again in early 2025.

CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. followed up with a June 9 video posted to social media warning of an impending crackdown.

“If those hospitals do not come into compliance and transparently display their prices to patients, they will be fined to the fullest extent the law allows,” Oz said.

“The grace period has ended,” Kennedy said.

Hospitals are supposed to post machine-readable files with pricing information, as well as consumer-friendly lists of hundreds of services that include either dollar prices or a price-estimator tool. The disclosures cover rates negotiated with insurers as well as the hospital's gross list prices and the discounted cash price available to patients paying without insurance.

Fisher’s group analyzes the websites of hospitals every year to evaluate how many are following the rules. About half of hospitals surveyed are technically complying with the regulation, but most of those are skirting the spirit of the law by posting percentages or algorithms. Federal rules allow hospitals to do so when prices cannot be expressed as a dollar amount.

Around one-third of surveyed hospitals were technically compliant in 2024, up from 16% in 2022, according to the group’s annual reports.

Trump issued an executive order last year calling for hospitals and insurance companies to make it easier to view and compare prices. Earlier this year, CMS updated the regulation to specify that if hospitals list algorithms instead of dollar prices, the public must still be able to derive the dollar amount.

Andrew Bremberg, who helped write the transparency rule at the White House Domestic Policy Council, said he had expected that getting hospitals to obey the rules would take time.

“My perspective has been that when you do something like this, they’re not going to comply, and what it’s going to take is a set period of steady enforcement by CMS,” said Bremberg, who is now a policy adviser to PatientRightsAdvocate.org.

He and Fisher stress that getting hospitals to post actual dollar amounts is critical so that patients can shop around and compare prices.

“I will call them out until the cows come home for us to see these prices,” Fisher said.

entries.title: Democrats’ Hollywood Allies Think the Party Has Lost the Plot
entries.summary: A number of entertainment industry figures who worked on Democrats’ successful 2018 cycle are sitting this one out.
entries.content:
Some of the Hollywood figures who helped Democrats retake the House in 2018 are reluctant to help them do it again.

Screenwriters, directors and other entertainment industry figures who once coached Democratic candidates, wrote their speeches and helped run rapid response operations are, at best, unmotivated to help this cycle and, at worst, entirely disillusioned with the party. Still, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ camp has been turning to industry types as a messaging resource, but some executives are upset that leaders can’t control the caucus’ growing progressive wing.

“The Democratic Party right now is torn in a couple directions, and some of those directions I'm no longer willing to work for or countenance, and so I'm a lot more sparing about it,” Gregg Hurwitz, a novelist and screenwriter known for his thriller series “Orphan X,” told The Washington Sun.

Hurwitz is part of a band of entertainment industry screenwriters, directors and producers who helped Democrats pick up 40 seats to gain control of the House in 2018. He said he worked pro bono writing and producing ads and coming up with a framework for moderate messaging that, he argued, “moves people away from the far left and right extremism.”

Hurwitz worked with Democratic campaigns between 2015 and 2022 but said he decided to leave the party after helping former Rep. Dean Phillips (D-Minnesota) challenge President Joe Biden in the 2024 primary. He cited the fact that Phillips faced attacks for raising concerns about Biden’s age and said vendors associated with Phillips were met with threats of being blacklisted for life — behavior he compared to the Chinese Communist Party.

He officially signed paperwork to change his party affiliation from Democrat to independent last fall.

For Hurwitz, the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America and “having candidates winning primaries now who have stated overtly that America is worse than Hamas and that white women are ‘ugly colonialist women,’” is not behavior he could condone, he said. “To me, it’s a measure of extremism that the left has permitted without drawing a line that is incredibly threatening.”

Now, the self-described liberal said he’s instead limiting his messaging strategies to more moderate Democrats and even some Republicans — including those within the Trump administration. Hurwitz declined to provide names.

“Now and then I will get a call from people on either side. It could be someone in the current administration, and if I'm convinced that they’re doing something that will benefit the American people, especially anyone who’s working class, I’m open to helping.” Hurwitz said.

Similarly, Marshall Herskovitz, a screenwriter and director known for creating the television shows “Thirtysomething” and “My So-Called Life,” said that he’s done dealing with Democrats. After President Donald Trump was reelected in 2024, Democrats, he told The Sun, “seemed just absolutely incapable of dealing with the size of the disaster.”
20260905_Herskovitz_018 copy 2.jpg (3937x2624, AR: 1.50)“I no longer try to work within the apparatus of the party, which is what I did in 2018, 2020, ’22, making commercials and doing position papers that they could use or not use, that sort of thing,” Herskovitz said. He criticized the current party structure as “ossified” and told The Sun the party “basically exists to keep the same people employed.”

Instead, Herskovitz is focused on helping Democrats who he connects with organically and not through official party channels. He has met with Democratic donors and with podcast creators about developing a project where he could communicate his vision for the party.

“Since Trump was elected again, and when I saw what Democrats were doing and not doing, I just came to realize that if there were going to be any answers, it was going to come from outside the party,” Herskovitz said.

He said about the fissure between Hollywood and current Democratic leaders: “It’s sad. It shouldn’t have to be this way.”

Another filmmaker who requested anonymity since they still work with some Democratic candidates said much of the frustration comes from the language used, rather than the policies. 

“Only Democrats have a hard time with it, OK? And that’s because we tend to speak in these cotton candy terms that sound like they were dreamed up in the Harvard faculty lounge,” the filmmaker said. “No one in the world says ‘bodily autonomy,’ they just don’t. Nobody says ‘unhoused’ when they mean ‘homeless.’ Nobody says ‘justice impacted individual’ when they mean ‘criminal.’ And no farmer in history ever woke up, looked at his wife and said, ‘I’m having an affordability issue.’”

Not all screenwriters and producers that worked with Democrats in the past are mad at the party — but they also aren’t rushing to help. 

Shawn Ryan, a screenwriter and producer known for his shows “The Night Agent” and “S.W.A.T.”, worked with Hurwitz and Herskovitz in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic making ads for political groups. He stopped working directly with Democrats because he “was just super busy with work,” Ryan told The Sun. His involvement in politics now, he said, revolves around donating to candidates he likes.

“I’m not looking to sort of bash Democrats at the moment. Republicans have always had more discipline in their messaging than Democrats. Democrats are just a messier sort of group, but they’re also, I think, a little bit more dedicated to good governing,” Ryan said.

But, Ryan added, he understood the aggravations of Hurwitz, Herkovitz and the other filmmaker. 

“They have the ear of a lot of people in the Democratic Party, so I think that’s where their frustration comes from,” Ryan said. “We’re used to, as writers, really thinking long and hard about the exact perfect word, and when we hear people saying imperfect words when the stakes are so high, of course it’s of frustration.”

Jeffries’ Ties to Hollywood Can Be Traced Back to 2018 

Despite these screenwriters’ criticism, Democrats are running back to the entertainment industry for advice now that they see the majority within reach.

Jeffries’ team has hosted at least two meetings with screenwriters to discuss messaging ahead of the midterms, The Sun has learned.

His office invited a select group of chiefs of staff to meet with “Hollywood TV producers and screenwriters who are offering support to House Democrats” in the Capitol in April 2025, according to an invite sent to congressional offices viewed by The Sun. And in July, House Democratic staffers again met with screenwriters in New York to “refine and expand” their messaging, according to a Democratic strategist familiar with the matter.

A spokesperson for Jeffries did not comment.

In addition to staff-led meetings, Jeffries has been a guest on non-political podcasts, like “Men in Blazers” and “The Dan Le Batard Show.” He's also talked about Jay-Z on The Ringer's “The Press Box.”

During the 2018 election cycle, Jeffries was co-chair of House Democratic leadership’s messaging arm, and he developed connections with Hollywood executives to craft the caucus’s communications.

“Our mission was to create the right messaging that would lead to us winning back the majority. And I have been communicating with screenwriters regularly since then,” former Illinois Rep. Cheri Bustos, who served as House Democratic Policy and Communications Committee co-chair with Jeffries at the time, told The Sun.

“They know how to tell stories compellingly, emotionally and movingly. They use the right words, the right tone and the right feel,” Bustos continued. “I can’t think of any better writers and storytellers than the screenwriters, directors and authors who I have worked with through Democratic politics.”
20260905_Herskovitz_046 copy.jpg (5411x3335, AR: 1.62)Democratic leaders also connected candidates to producers in 2018. Former Rep. Harley Rouda of California, who defeated a Republican incumbent at the time, told The Sun that candidates in the House Democrats’ flagship ‘Red to Blue’ program “had access to people in Hollywood.” Screenwriters did not just consult candidates, they were directly involved with their communication operations.

“The concept was pretty simple: They are excellent storytellers, that’s what they do for a living, and the best way to connect with voters was to be able to tell a compelling story with compelling messaging that hopefully allows you the opportunity to win the race,” Rouda said.

He added, “Prior to 2018, Hollywood and the film industry predominantly were supporters of Democratic causes and candidates with their checkbooks.” Rouda said Trump’s 2016 election prompted filmmakers to actually get involved.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which handles the ‘Red to Blue’ program, downplayed any coordination, saying in a statement, it “does not connect screenwriters to our campaigns.”

“Our mission has been recruiting candidates with working backgrounds who listen to the voters directly. What they are hearing is that the American people are pissed at House Republicans and their broken promises — it’s easy to see why folks from all walks of life are raising their hand and asking how they can help Democrats take back the House,” said DCCC spokesperson Viet Shelton.

The anonymous filmmaker who is still working with Democrats told The Sun they have written speeches “for a ton” of candidates and have been flown “from state to state to do candidate training” by “private individuals” or some state Democratic parties. The filmmaker declined to say which candidates they are working with. 

“This is literally half of my day. This is the unpaid half of my day. It’s helping Democrats learn how to sound less like Democrats, so that they can make the argument that independent voters can actually hear,” the filmmaker said.

One House Democrat who has worked directly with the filmmaker told The Sun that the filmmaker has met with politicians for one-on-one meetings at the Beverly Hills Tennis Club, an exclusive, members-only club frequented by celebrities.

Hollywood to Dems: Stop Saying ‘Affordability’ 

In addition to in-person coaching sessions, the filmmaker also sends emails to dozens of Democratic lawmakers and candidates with messaging advice. The Sun viewed over half a dozen emails they had sent this election cycle, including one where they advised Democrats to stay away from their favorite word: “affordability.”

“I HATE the word affordability. No one in the real world says it. No farmer in history ever said to his wife, ‘I’m having a real affordability crisis lately.’ It’s another cotton-candy Democrat word,” the filmmaker wrote. “Try THIS instead: The Cost of Trump.”

“This can mean higher prices for eggs, gas, diesel, fertilizer, insurance, utilities. It can mean the closing of rural hospitals, the end of Medicaid, the rise of A.I. without any guardrails,” they added. “The list is endless — but ALL of these things are The COST OF TRUMP. I just tried this phrase on a breakfast attended by 20 people. It CRUSHED.”

In another email, with the subject line “WHITE POVERTY,” the filmmaker wrote: “Among the many poor and low-income voters in the US, 66 million are white. They comprise 40% of the electorate in swing states. They largely voted for Biden in 2020 and then stayed home in 2024.”

“Kamala [Harris] tried to sell joy to people who couldn't afford eggs. And we made things worse by correcting their pronouns,” they added. “All they really want is someone who will go to bat for their families in real and meaningful ways.”

And in a third email, the filmmaker urged Democrats to stop saying that Congress did not approve Trump’s war in Iran because it “sounds like whining.”

Democrats should instead say that “we are better off” without the Islamic Republic of Iran, the filmmaker wrote, but that Trump is not the person to lead because his policies “have been catastrophic.”

The House Democrat who spoke to The Sun said that some of the emails are “very eccentric but I read them and they’re helpful.”

Still, some Democrats were quick to downplay filmmakers’ involvement in the party’s messaging.
House Dems 11/12/25 (7857x5196, AR: 1.51)In 2011, after Democrats lost control of the House, then-Leader Nancy Pelosi met with people in the film industry to discuss ideas about how they could win back the majority, the former DCCC official said. But, they added, Pelosi took these meetings because “It wasn’t just Nancy Pelosi wanting to hear people’s thoughts, it was Nancy Pelosi doing very important donor maintenance.”

“Let’s just say that when I got briefed on the results of these sessions, they were not things that we ran and shared with our candidates because they just weren’t relevant,” the official said. Pelosi’s office did not respond to The Sun’s requests for comment.

Another Democratic consultant who has extensive experience with the intersection of actors, screenwriters and politicians said that sentiment continues in the 2026 election cycle.

“I don’t need them for comms strategy, I need them for their fucking fame and money,” the consultant told The Sun. “After all, the last thing any campaign needs is another cook in the kitchen when writing talking points.”

entries.title: How Virginia Could Smoke Out D.C.’s Cannabis Industry
entries.summary: The city’s retailers stand to lose cross-border business when Virginia begins recreational sales next summer.
entries.content:
Johannes Cassidy-Seyoum opened his medical cannabis business in D.C. just last year. Already, he’s bracing for a devastating blow to his customer base.

Across the Potomac, Virginia lawmakers in June approved the sale of recreational cannabis beginning in July 2027. The move will upend the region’s cannabis market, which has historically seen Virginians travel to D.C. to access the city’s permissive medical program in which anyone over 21 can “self-certify” as a user.

Cannabis business owners in D.C., who already took a hit when Maryland began recreational sales in 2023, fear for their livelihoods.

“Virginia coming online will definitely, probably take 20% to 25% of our business,” said Cassidy-Seyoum, the owner of High Demand in Capitol Hill. “A good amount of our customers come from Richmond, Fredericksburg. They make a trip maybe two, three times a month and they stock up.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Virginia will issue 350 recreational retail licenses to cannabis businesses in February through a lottery system, with a portion set aside for smaller operators. The goal is to capture the business of both Virginia’s underground cannabis market and customers who shop in neighboring jurisdictions. The state expects its cannabis sales tax to generate $71 million in its first two years.

“We’re very concerned, our store is right on the border around Virginia,” said Caroline Crandall, who owns Green Theory in the Palisades. “Virginia and a lot of other southern states account for a decent portion of sales every month.”

Of the 2,101 non-D.C. residents who patronized D.C. cannabis retailers in July, 807 came from Virginia, according to a report from D.C.’s Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Administration.

Maryland’s cannabis regulator does not track such metrics, but about half of Virginia’s medical cannabis patients reported going out of state to purchase cannabis, according to an October 2024 survey conducted by Virginia’s Cannabis Control Authority. A quarter of those respondents said their destination was D.C. and one-fifth said it was Maryland.

That could devastate “an already difficult business,” said Greg Casten, president of the restaurant group OceanPro Industries, who’s in the permitting process to open a dispensary in Northeast D.C.

“It’s just a very scrappy time. Rent is high in D.C.,” said Allison Lipowitz, the manager of District Cannabis’ storefront in NoMa. “I think that’s why Virginia feels so scary — it’s already a very unstable market.”

Some business owners feel helpless. District voters overwhelmingly approved marijuana legalization in 2014, but Congress has blocked that from happening.

"D.C. currently lacks the democratic autonomy to enact laws affecting its own local markets without interference from federal policymakers,” Chinyere Hubbard, the president and CEO of the D.C. Chamber of Commerce, told The Sun in a statement. “That disparity leaves District businesses competing on an uneven playing field with our neighboring jurisdictions.”

Since 2014, hundreds of businesses operated in a “gray market” by “gifting” cannabis alongside clothing, food or even motivational speeches out of gift stores, gas stations and delivery services. When the District began its self-certified medical program in 2022, it gave those businesses a window in which they could get licensed — 45 of them did.

That program, for residents, made cannabis almost as easily obtainable as it might be in a recreational market. But out-of-towners still need to pay at least $10 in fees to purchase it. Business owners have long wanted to scrap that, reduce it, or — better yet — have cannabis federally rescheduled — something Robbie Martin, president of the D.C. Cannabis Business Association, said is closer to happening than ever.

“We have a lot more restrictions in D.C. right now than Virginia will next year,” Crandall said. “[We’re trying to] figure out ways to remain competitive. One of those is hoping and praying that rescheduling of adult-use cannabis ends up happening.”
_MG_7822 copy.jpg (5452x3635, AR: 1.50)There are other ways D.C. businesses might keep their edge. Some are trying to get permits to add on-site consumption spaces to their dispensaries, Martin said. Martin runs one such a site: Higher Ground in Northeast D.C., a converted distillery stylishly outfitted with leather couches, deep green walls, artful glasswork and even a café space he hopes will soon sell sandwiches, coffee and other “munchies.” On a Tuesday afternoon last week, one customer was using it as a co-working space.

“We have a big competitive advantage in D.C.,” Martin said. “There’s very few places in the country, let alone the East Coast, with this capability.”

What’s more, Virginia is entering the marketplace with problems of its own. Existing medical dispensaries will have to pay a one-time $10 million conversion fee to become licensed as recreational facilities.

That’s “especially concerning” to JM Pedini, the development director of the National Organization for the Reform of Marijuana Laws.

“These are the operators currently serving Virginia's medical cannabis patients, and the law effectively conditions their ability to continue operating on paying that fee,” Pedini said. “We should be protecting patient access and affordability during this transition, not introducing a new eight-figure cost into the medical supply chain."

Virginia has seen more than $107 million in medical cannabis sales this year as of early August, but the state’s illicit market could be worth between $1.5 billion and $3 billion, said Trent Woloveck, the chief strategy officer at Jushi Holdings. Woloveck’s company operates 42 cannabis dispensaries across eight states including Virginia, and recently launched a $50 million expansion in Manassas on the back of the legalization announcement.

That could convert to the regulated marketplace. States adopting recreational cannabis laws see both a 45% reduction in law enforcement seizures of the drug (which could either indicate a smaller illegal marketplace, or a shift in law enforcement priorities), said Nicole Fitzgerald, a postdoctoral fellow at Columbia University who studies illegal drug markets.

Those states also see a 9% reduction in street prices, said Angelica Meinhofer, an assistant professor at Weill Cornell Medical College who specializes in health economics.

As further incentive, Virginia has kept its initial sales tax rate low at 6%, though municipalities can levy an additional tax of up to 3.5%. Maryland’s, by contrast, is 12%. D.C.’s tax rate is also 6%.

While D.C. businesses brainstorm ways to keep their customers, Virginia municipalities are gearing up to welcome more tax revenue, job creation and redirected sales. In Fairfax, Woloveck’s company Jushi already has a medical dispensary that Colleen Kardasz, Fairfax’s director of economic development, expects will become a recreational facility.

The city is currently evaluating how to zone recreational dispensaries as well as how to tax them, but Kardasz said she expects legalization to keep cannabis-related business in the community.

“People like convenience,” Kardasz said. “If you can get something in your own community, you’re going to choose that over traveling.”

Consumers aren’t the only ones who might choose to do business in Virginia instead of D.C.

“We are planning to hopefully expand into Virginia,” Crandall said, adding that she’ll apply for a license as soon as they open. “We’re probably not the only ones to do so.”
