entries.title: New Technology, New Ideas: How the Nationals Overhauled Their Farm System
entries.summary: While the Nats stagger to the finish line, the franchise’s minor league teams are surging.
entries.content:
On July 7 — an otherwise unremarkable day for the Washington Nationals, who lost an unremarkable game to the Houston Astros in the middle of a mostly unremarkable summer at Nationals Park — something remarkable happened in the minor leagues.

In stadiums in Erie, Pennsylvania, and Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, four hitters from the Harrisburg Senators and Fredericksburg Nationals — the Nats’ Double-A and Single-A affiliates, respectively — all bashed home runs. The significance: With those four homers, Washington’s six minor league teams, collectively, had surpassed the total of 409 homers hit by those same affiliates in 2025.

And it was barely past the midpoint of the 2026 baseball calendar.

As the Nationals limp to the finish line of the MLB season, all but assured of a seventh-straight finish in either fourth or fifth place, fans of the team would be well advised to avert their eyes from Nationals Park and train them on the minor leagues, where remarkable things continue to happen.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

It is there that the organization’s transformation from a largely old-school operation under former president of baseball operations Mike Rizzo to a largely new-school model under successor Paul Toboni is most visible, with the new regime leaning heavily into advanced analytics and new technologies geared toward succeeding in a sport increasingly distilled to a clash of power-pitching versus power-hitting.

To wit: With roughly two weeks left in the minor league season, the collective home run total for the Nats’ six affiliates is up to 681 (through Sept. 8), a staggering increase of nearly 67% over 2025’s total. The system-wide slugging percentage has similarly risen from .349 to .410. All six Nats’ affiliates have seen a jump in their home run totals year over year.

On the pitching side, according to data at Prospect Savant, Nats’ prospects have pushed the farm system’s collective strikeout rate (the percentage of all plate appearances ending in a strikeout) from 21.7 in 2025 (28th out of 30 farm systems) to 24.1 in 2026 (seventh). And the system’s collective ERA of 4.58 is the best of any MLB franchise.

And what about the bottom line, which is to say: wins and losses? Collectively, the Nationals’ four-highest affiliates (Single-A Fredericksburg, high Single-A Wilmington, Double-A Harrisburg and Triple-A Rochester) have a winning percentage of .560 this season (through Sept. 8), up from .452 in 2025, with Rochester (up from .401 to .606, year over year) responsible for much of that improvement.

“It’s completely independent of what the previous regime did or did not do,” Toboni, 36, said when asked about the link between the massive organizational overhaul and the sudden turnaround of the farm system. The Rizzo regime, he said, “did a bunch of awesome things. Obviously, there’s a bunch of players on our roster that came from them. For us, it’s a completely separate conversation … For us, it’s: ‘Let’s tether ourselves to what the evidence says contributes to winning and do our best to actually help our people get there.’”

Paul Toboni AP - 25321818817757 (6748x4499, AR: 1.50)
The rest of the industry is certainly taking note. In its 2026 midseason farm-system rankings, released in mid-August, MLB Pipeline had the Nationals ranked sixth out of all 30 organizations, up from 17th at the start of the season and 23rd at midseason 2025. Similar double-digit jumps were seen in rankings compiled by Baseball America, ESPN and Fangraphs.

There are caveats begging to be noted here: First, a majority of players in the Nats’ farm system, including most of its highest-rated prospects, were acquired by the Rizzo regime, before he was fired last July. Also, teams such as the Nationals that are undergoing a rebuild — which typically result in veterans-for-prospects trades and high draft picks — almost always see a rise in their farm-system rankings.

But the sheer speed and acuteness of the Nationals’ rise in those rankings, in the first year of a new regime whose overarching philosophy represents an organizational sea change, makes it impossible to ignore those links. At his introductory press conference last October, Toboni vowed to turn the Nats into a “scouting and player development monster,” and less than a year in (thanks in part to trades of veterans Jose A. Ferrer, MacKenzie Gore, Luis García Jr. and Foster Griffin), he appears to be well on his way.

“To rise 17 spots in a calendar year, or 11 spots from the beginning of the year — that is highly unusual,” said MLB Pipeline senior writer Jim Callis, who has been evaluating prospects for various publications for 38 years. “You talk to anybody in the game, and [they would say] the Nats have modernized in a lot of ways. They’ve introduced a lot of technology and data. I don’t mean to make it sound like they were in the dark ages under Rizzo — because Mike was really good there for a long time, which people sometimes forget — but I do think [Toboni and his staff] have modernized a lot of things, and they’ve seen some players make huge steps forward.”

Abimelec Ortiz Rochester AP - 26149699752550 (4000x2667, AR: 1.50)

Speaking the Same Language


Some of the changes under the Toboni regime are easy to document. Whereas the front office and player-development staffs under Rizzo (who was 63 when he was fired) were full of longtime scouts and grizzled baseball lifers, Toboni has tapped the collegiate ranks and new-school, data-driven facilities (as well as other MLB organizations) in search of innovators. Of particular note: At least four of Toboni’s hires, including Nationals pitching coach Simon Mathews, spent time at Driveline Baseball, the groundbreaking, Seattle-based lab.

“We wanted to bring in people who were data-informed — not data-driven on every decision — and then we built out training environments that helped players get better,” said assistant general manager Devin Pearson. “We didn’t say, ‘We need to bring in X number of people from Driveline’ or whatever. It was more: ‘Do we all speak the same language and believe in the same things in terms of what good training looks like.”

The Nationals also acquired — at a reported cost of $15,000 to $20,000 per month apiece, with three-year-minimum leases — three high-tech Trajekt Arc pitching machines that use video, data and robotics to replicate the image, velocity, pitch-shape and arm slot of any pitcher in baseball, allowing hitters to take virtual BP against each night’s opposing starter. The team was believed to have been the last MLB franchise without at least one Trajekt machine.

“It’s like night and day,” Nationals outfielder Daylen Lile said of the analytics bent of the new regime. (That’s a more charitable characterization than what he said to Sirius MLB Network Radio during spring training: “We’re not in the dark ages anymore.”)

The investment in player development doesn’t stop at technology. The Lerner family, who have owned the Nationals since 2006, also green-lighted a massive expansion of minor league staffing under Toboni. The field staff at Triple-A Rochester, for example, has doubled in size from 2025, with the addition of assistant hitting and pitching coaches, a quality control coach, a defensive coach, an extra strength coach, an extra trainer and a technician to operate the Trajekt machine. Meanwhile, Rochester manager Matt LeCroy, a longtime Rizzo lieutenant, was kept on following a lengthy meeting with Toboni.

“From the beginning it was all about everybody buying in. Paul told you up-front: If you weren’t in, you would probably be out,” said LeCroy, who has been part of the Nationals organization, off and on, since 2006. LeCroy’s Red Wings have surged from 59-88 last year to 83-54 so far in 2026. “It’s been amazing to see this thing grow so fast and to see all this change. I’ve learned so much this year,” he said.

Matt LeCroy AP - 26122031238347 (4000x2667, AR: 1.50)

A Clear Vision

Beyond some of the obvious factors, other aspects of the new regime’s special sauce are harder to get at. Toboni and his lieutenants are understandably cautious with what they reveal about their methods and strategies.

“What it boils down to is having a really clear vision of what you want to achieve and a staff that is incredibly aligned, and then doing a really good job of communicating to the players what the greatest opportunities are for them to get better,” Toboni said. “I think maybe it was a lot for the players [to absorb] early on, but now I think they’ve felt the cadence and understand the process well enough to realize: ‘OK, I need to strike out more batters. OK, to do that I’ve got to refine my breaking ball. OK, in this bullpen session, I need my slider to have this much horizontal movement and this much vertical.’”

Twenty-three-year-old shortstop prospect Seaver King is perhaps the Toboni player-development machine’s biggest success story, a microcosm of the organization’s collective rise. In 2025, his first full year of pro ball, King, the 10th overall pick in the 2024 draft, hit just .244 with a .631 OPS, six homers in 551 plate appearances, and a strikeouts-to-walks ratio of more than four-to-one across two levels of the minors.

In his first meeting with the Nats’ new player-development staff, King was astonished to hear a detailed, advanced-metrics-heavy rundown of his assets and liabilities and a specific plan for improvement — focused on lowering his chase rate (swinging at pitches outside of the strike zone) and raising his launch angle. Defensively, he needed tweaks to his arm slot and footwork. It was almost as if they knew him better as a player than he did himself.

“It was a matter of being told, ‘Hey, this is what we think is going to make you successful,’ and then buying into it,” King said. “And the message has stayed consistent at every level: ‘We don’t want you to chase . We want you to hit the ball hard in the air.’... I’ve always hit the ball hard, but I’ve gotten away with hitting it on the ground and getting hits with my speed. But now I know, if I hit the ball at 12 [degrees of launch angle] instead of six, I could have 10 to 12 more doubles than I did last year.”

It’s not as if launch angle were a foreign concept under the old regime, King said. “We heard about it: ‘Hey, we’d like you to hit the ball in the air,’” he said. “But there was never [any guidance] like, ‘Here’s how we can train for it.’”

This season, which King has split between Double-A and Triple-A, his batting average (through Sept. 8) is more than 60 points (to .306) and his OPS more nearly 280 points (to .909), while his strikeouts-to-walks ratio has been cut in half to just above two-to-one. His chase rate of 33.4 this season (per Prospect Savant) is still high — the big-league average this year is 30.5 — but it’s a considerable improvement over 2025’s mark of 36.0.

“The process has changed,” King said. “What makes me good is when I hit the ball hard and hit it in the air. If I can hit it in the air, extra-base hits will come. RBIs will come. Leaning into that and focusing on that in [batting practice] has been great, and obviously the results speak for themselves.”

As impressive as it was for the Nationals to top their collective minor league home run total from 2025 on July 7 of this year, King got there some five weeks sooner: On May 30, he hit his seventh homer of the year, beating his 2025 total in just 44 games. He is a near-lock to be on the Nationals’ roster by next Opening Day.

entries.title: Jayden Daniels Is Preparing for His Next Act
entries.summary: Coming off a rough sophomore season, Washington’s star quarterback is looking to recapture the magic of 2024.
entries.content:
There are many lies out there.

Honesty isn’t always the best policy. The run doesn’t always set up the pass. And sometimes you do get a second chance to make a first impression.

For Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels, the 2024 season was about as good a first impression as one could have. Twelve wins. Rookie of the Year award. A Hail Mary against the Bears. One game away from the Super Bowl.

But one truth? What goes up must come down. And in 2025, Washington crash-landed back to earth as Daniels missed more games than he played and the team finished 5-12.

An ugly season, coupled with an uneven end to training camp this summer, and questions start forming. Was 2024 a fluke? Did defenses figure Daniels out?

For his part, Daniels has said all the right things about moving on from last year and putting in the work to improve himself. His coaches have raved about his accuracy and football IQ. His teammates talk about him like the 2024 season — not 2025 — was the last they saw of the quarterback.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

While it’s unclear what the coming season will bring, one thing feels certain in Ashburn: This is Jayden Daniels 2.0.

“What I did Year 1, what I did Year 2 doesn’t really matter,” Daniels said ahead of the team’s Week 1 matchup against the Eagles. “Now we’re onto Year 3. Whatever happens Sunday, that’s what people are going to talk about.”

Let the Commanders tell it, and Daniels has put in his 10,000 hours. He’s constantly tinkering with the minutiae of the game, working with each receiver after practices on where to sit down on a route, when to make a move on a defender and how they like to receive the ball. Whether he’s sending a film clip to receiver Terry McLaurin or engaging in a scheme discussion with new offensive coordinator David Blough, Daniels is working to be in full command of Washington’s offense.

Jayden Daniels AP - 26234555802029 (2933x1955, AR: 1.50)Daniels has looked sharp on the field, dropping the ball in the bucket to his receivers like a ceiling leak. On timing routes, the ball is out of Daniels’ hand the second he hits his third step. His over-the-shoulder passes end up where only his receivers can grab them.

“It’s the location of the throw. It’s one of his superpowers, is the accuracy,” coach Dan Quinn said last month. “That’s not luck.”

Blough, entering his first season as offensive coordinator after two years as assistant quarterbacks coach, agreed.

“He’s as accurate as he’s ever been,” Blough said. “It’s a testament to asking him to do something different and him wanting to grow and evolve.”

Blough’s offense will call for more play-action and bootlegs with the hope that getting Daniels outside of the pocket will lead to more downfield throws. He’ll be tasked with making more pre-snap reads and changing plays at the line of scrimmage. All while operating more under center, which he has done just 32 times through his first two seasons, according to the Commanders.

“Day by day, I just try to come in and have control of the offense and get 1% better,” Daniels said during camp.

But his coaches have raved about how quickly he’s picked up a new system. Quinn has repeatedly said he was taken aback by Daniels’ ability to get up to speed.

“He often makes the difficult things look easy,” Quinn said in July.

Evolution in the passing game will be a priority this season, as the Commanders look to rely less on Daniels’s running abilities. In 2024 and 2025, Daniels had the third-most rushing attempts by a quarterback (206) despite playing in just 24 games.

He’s also taken some nasty hits: In his first two seasons, Daniels broke a rib, sprained his left knee, strained his right hamstring and dislocated his left elbow.

Quinn has encouraged Daniels to live to fight another day by throwing the ball away rather than risk contact. The quarterback understands that advice, but is mindful that his legs — which he calls his “God capabilities” — are just as valuable as his right arm.

“Myself, anybody around would say they still want me to use [my legs] as a weapon. I’m pretty sure fans would say the same thing,” Daniels told The Washington Sun. “I don't want to sit back there and not be myself, but also just be smart with the opportunities and the chances I take.

“At the end of the day, I still play football. I still have a job to do to help my team win games, and if that’s taking off on third-and-3 and getting a first down instead of sitting back there and trying to make something happen, I’m gonna do it.”
Jayden Daniels Netflix AP - 25341652029435 (7800x5200, AR: 1.50)Daniels spent the offseason strengthening his entire body, particularly his legs, core and hips. He told The Sun he added “eight to 10 pounds” of muscle. But they may be hard to spot: Ever since Daniels was a 135-pound freshman in high school, there has been skepticism around his weight.

He’s too skinny. His body won’t hold up. He needs some milk.

Daniels, currently listed at 6-foot-4 and 210 pounds, said it’s all a misconception.

“I think it’s more so my build,” he said. “I'm heavier than a lot of people actually give me credit for. I’m just a taller, slender guy.”

If his listed weights are accurate, Daniels has gained over 50 pounds since weighing 157 pounds his senior year of high school in 2018. He sees no reason to put on too much additional muscle.

“Not really looking to be like a bodybuilder or anything like that,” he said.

Daniels may not want to be Mr. Olympia, but he is striving to move past his first two seasons.

He does his best to ignore the analysts and pundits who believe the Commanders will sink to the bottom of the NFC East this year, choosing to maintain his approach of never getting too high or too low. He believes that returning to the successes of 2024 will require a focus on his day-to-day process rather than chasing a specific result.

“I don’t want to be my final product in Week 1,” he said. “I just want to go out there and continue to just get better each and every day, each and every game and do whatever it takes to help the team win some football games.”

entries.title: DMV High School Volleyball Players of the Week
entries.summary: Our first group of the season features standouts from West Springfield, Bishop O’Connell and Marshall.
entries.content:
A new fall season marks a fresh start for the D.C. area’s top high school volleyball programs. With the slate wiped clean, local powers have begun jockeying for position. The season is already in full swing in Virginia, while matches are just getting underway in Maryland and D.C. Here are three players who have made strong early impressions:

Anna Dierks, Senior, Setter, West Springfield

The Spartans are on a quest to repeat as Virginia Class 6 champions after earning the first state crown in program history last season. Dierks, who brought a steadying presence to West Springfield’s attack during its title run, is one of several key returners for coach Stephanie Noriega’s team. With Dierks back at setter for her senior season, West Springfield got off to a 6-0 start, dropping just one set. In that span, Dierks averaged 9.4 assists per set and amassed 25 serving aces.

Against fellow Class 6 contender Marshall in late August, Dierks dished 35 assists in a dominant three-set sweep. Many of those assists were lobbed to senior Milena Kibret, who racked up 15 kills. With Dierks commanding the offense and a plethora of size and versatility on the block, the Spartans look more than capable of defending their title.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Macie Murray, Senior, Outside Hitter, Bishop O’Connell

The Knights are one of the buzziest teams in the area this season, thanks to a roster that is loaded with Division I talent. Murray, O’Connell’s veteran outside hitter, is off to a dazzling start this season. The senior averaged 4.2 kills per set and hit at an efficient .528 percent clip through the team’s first six matches.

The Knights kicked off their season with a 3-0 sweep of fellow Washington Catholic Athletic Conference contender Holy Cross, then swept each of their opponents at the Virginia Volleyball Showcase over the weekend. Murray, sophomore setter Carolyn Maria and freshman outside hitter Nadia Wooten were each named to the all-tournament team.

Ayla Sayd, Senior, Outside Hitter, Marshall

Sayd notched double-digit kills in each of Marshall’s first seven matches of the fall, announcing herself as one of the most potent offensive threats in the area early this season. The 6-foot-1 senior, who is committed to Elon, amassed 111 kills in 23 sets played to get the Statesmen off to a 6-1 start.

The team is under new leadership this season with coach Allie Selznick taking over the varsity program — and with Sayd anchoring the Marshall attack, the Statesmen look poised to make a Virginia Class 6 run. ”Even from last year to this year, she’s grown tremendously,” Selznick said of Sayd. “She’s really come into her own [and] become a powerhouse.”

entries.title: Talk to Tom: Thoughts on Rye Bunny, Corkage Fees and Cramped Tables
entries.summary: Plus: Recommendations for a great culinary road trip close to D.C.
entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining-advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space.

Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@washingtonsun.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

Few of us are string beans. Why do restaurants set tables so close to one another? 

Not that I want to return to pandemic times, but there was a moment then where we enjoyed pools of space between our fellow diners, a detail that’s now mostly the reserve of high-end restaurants with lofty prices. Like hush, room to stretch out is a luxury.

Restaurants pack people in mostly for financial reasons. More tables per square foot mean more potential revenue. I once had a local restaurateur tell me removing just a single table from his business would result in the loss of “hundreds of thousands of dollars” a year. There’s the buzz factor, too. A tightly packed dining room tends to feel more energetic, no doubt because people are talking louder to compensate for the conversations close to them.

The position carries some risks, and not just from people trying to navigate slivers of space. A 2009 study by Cornell University called “Don’t Sit So Close to Me” found customers were significantly happier when tables were placed at least a meter apart, and diners at cramped tables left faster and reported they were less likely to return — especially on dates and among women, who reported more discomfort than men. A follow-up study two years later tested 6-inch, foot-long, and 24-inch spacing of tables and determined that people reacted particularly poorly to the lack of space in romantic dining contexts.

There’s no industry standard for spacing. But an expert in restaurant design psychology told me 16 inches is a minimum to aim for at banquettes, which usually have the most space around them.

Curious what you think about the trade-off at Rye Bunny between the efficiency of the counter-order setup and the more relaxed rhythm one might want from a dinner out. 

For those who haven’t been, the first-come, first-served Rye Bunny is the successor to Tail Up Goat in Adams Morgan, which closed in December. While I’m not a fan of standing in line to access a table, the process has impressed me twice now at the breezy Rye Bunny, where staff members welcome you upon entry and take drink orders while you wait to reach a host counter to tell an attendant what you want for dinner. Then, off you go to select where you want to sit in the dining room.
DC0A4190 copy.jpg (7791x5193, AR: 1.50)DC0A4331 copy.jpg (7369x4912, AR: 1.50)FYI: I’ve never been in line longer than 10 minutes, which goes by fast with a drink in hand, and I’ve enjoyed some engaging chats with neighbors in line. Per the restaurant’s FAQ, waits are shortest (five to 15 minutes) Sunday through Thursday, with often no wait after 8:30 p.m. The idea is working for the restaurant. Co-owner Jill Tyler tells me some guests, unknown to one another when they stroll in, end up sitting together based on their brief interactions in line.

Want to order another drink or more food once you’re seated? Proceed as you would at another upscale restaurant and ask your server. And make sure to order the anchovy toast and whatever pasta your server raves about, among the draws on Rye Bunny’s script.

I collect wine and like to bring it to restaurants on occasion. What’s a fair corkage fee? Some are so high! 

Industry insiders tell me the answer depends on a number of factors, including the restaurant concept and the beverage program. An establishment with a small list might charge a lot less for corkage or waive it altogether as an incentive to customers. Places with larger, more curated lists might charge more — or forbid outside bottles completely.

“Sometimes they might not allow it because it can be difficult to deal with old bottles if you don’t have an Ah-So (a two-pronged wine opener that doesn’t break the cork) and an experienced sommelier,” says Brent Kroll, the owner of Maxwell Park Wine Bar and a veteran wine professional. “That and possibly that older bottles require time from the sommelier for minimal revenue.”

Jenistar Ruksirisopha created the wine lists for both Takara 14 and Raw Omakase in Logan Circle. At the casual Takara 14, where the wine and sake bottles typically cost between $20 and $80, she considered $50 per bottle a fair corkage fee; at the more refined Raw Omakase, where the bottles can range from $60 to $1,200, the restaurateur asked for $75 per bottle.

“The fee is not only opening and serving the bottle but also glassware, service, and the loss of beverage sales,” says Ruksirisopha, who is no longer involved with either restaurant but plans to open, with chef Johnny Yi, an upscale sushi venue sometime next year.

The corkage fee at the popular Reveler’s Hour in Adams Morgan is $50. Owner Bill Jensen says he has mixed feelings about diners bringing in their own wine. “I love the idea of enhancing a meal by sharing a special bottle of wine” from outside, he says, but “we go out of our way to curate a dynamic, expansive selection of wines to suit all sensibilities and budgets, and we want the opportunity to share it with our guests.”

Kroll allows corkage only for large parties where there’s a minimum spend. His rationale: “We have 50 wines by the glass and just under 1,000 by the bottle.” Outside his venue, he says, “I’m happy when I see $25 and think $50 (corkage fee) is OK.” Mark’s Duck House in Falls Church, Virginia, charges $20 a bottle, and the sibling D.C. restaurants Clyde’s and Old Ebbitt Grill charge $25. Some places don’t charge on certain days. For instance, Monday is the best time to bring a bottle from home at Belga Café on the Hill, which otherwise charges $25.

My two cents: The considerate wine consumer should know not to bring in a wine that’s on a restaurant’s list and to buy at least one bottle from the restaurant. Also, some restaurants have a limit on how many bottles you can bring in. It’s always best to call ahead and ask rather than be surprised upon arrival.

With the season about to change, I want to plan a road trip. Where would you go for a dining escape within a few hours of D.C.? (We already know about the Inn at Little Washington.)

In the exurbs of Virginia, I’m high on Three Blacksmiths in Sperryville. The drill is a single seating for up to 20 guests in a handsome dining room, and a seasonal, five-course menu prepared by chefs who double as your attendants by introducing the dishes to you. Orchestrated by owners Jake and Sara Addeo, the evening starts at 6:45 p.m. with a choice of cocktails (including a zero-proof option) made using local ingredients.

Then there’s Maude & the Bear in Staunton, which began life as a Montgomery Ward home kit more than a century ago, helmed by chef Ian Boden. He, too, offers a five-course list — along with nine- and 22-course tasting menus — that the chef says include “several little surprises.” My experience with Boden, who also owns The Shack nearby, is that he focuses on good ingredients left to speak for themselves.

In Maryland, I’m always happy to settle into the inviting, Old World interior at Bas Rouge in historic Easton. The restaurant is the crown jewel of Bluepoint Hospitality, a collection of 10 culinary draws created by energy mogul Paul Prager. The details at Bas Rouge are rich: Zalto stemware, Bernardaud china and an antique Lobmeyr crystal chandelier to illuminate the space. As for the cooking, Harley Peet won the Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic award from the James Beard Foundation two years ago. Peet, recently promoted to corporate executive chef, says his mission is to “continually elevate.” Some of the ingredients his team uses are plucked from the company’s fledgling Yamori Farm, 7 or so acres devoted to Japanese melons, radishes, leeks and more, watched over by Japanese farmers who fly in on a regular basis, says Peet.

entries.title: Denver Files Lawsuit to Bar Immigration Agents From Polling Places
entries.summary: DHS has not yet announced coordinated plans to deploy federal agents to the polls, though there have been at least two incidents in recent months.
entries.content:
The city of Denver and a coalition of advocacy groups asked a federal judge on Thursday to prohibit the Trump administration from deploying federal immigration agents to polling sites ahead of the November midterm elections.

The first-of-its-kind lawsuit asserts that allowing federal agents to serve warrants at polling locations violates federal laws that protect free elections. The filers asked the district court in Washington D.C. to prohibit federal officers from carrying weapons near voting locations or other polling sites, as well.

“It disrupts voting and makes it more difficult for state and local election officials and law enforcement to do their jobs by making polling places spaces of confrontation,” the lawsuit says.

The left-leaning group Democracy Forward filed the lawsuit alongside Denver, the League of United Latin American Citizens, Common Cause and Unidos US. The lawsuit specifically names Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and David Venturella, the acting head of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The Trump administration has not announced concrete plans for these kinds of deployments, but the lawsuit contends such a policy is coming down the pike.

In a statement on Thursday, Democracy Forward said that the policy was “confirmed and clarified” by Mullin “when he said that ICE officers could enter polling places to serve warrants or conduct other immigration and customs enforcement activity.”

The lawsuit specifically says that ICE agents entered a polling site in Syracuse, New York, in June to interview an election volunteer about a social media post, and in another case, agents “swarmed” the parking lot of a polling site in San Antonio to arrest a person there.

Mullin told reporters earlier this month that “ICE isn’t there to patrol the polling places,” but said that federal agents could be deployed in the case of a “threat” or to serve a specific warrant.

The lawsuit comes as early voting is set to begin in states across the country later this month with only weeks until the Nov. 3 elections.

Federal law bans military personnel or “armed” agents from election sites “unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Washington Sun.

entries.title: Security Experts Say NATO Must Plan for a Future Without the United States
entries.summary: As Russia appears to test NATO to see how the fractured group responds, European allies don’t know if they can continue to rely on the U.S.
entries.content:
BERLIN — Trump administration officials have made a flurry of visits to Moscow over the last month, with Europe on edge over a spate of hybrid attacks attributed to Russia.

But America’s European allies aren’t taking the visits as reassurance. Rather, security experts say they see it as another sign of the deep strain plaguing the NATO alliance.

American action is now less predictable, and its leaders are less communicative and less reliably committed to the NATO structure that has governed European security for 75 years, the experts said. Even if President Donald Trump doesn’t ultimately fulfill his threats to leave the alliance, the experts in the region said NATO needs to prepare to go it alone.

“There's very real concern here,” said Ian Lesser, a security analyst at the German Marshall Fund of the United States in Brussels. “One can debate why Russia is doing this. To keep NATO allies on edge? To create a sense of anxiety?”

He added: “Nonetheless, they are doing it. It is having effects. Europe is going to have to deal with this in a more deliberate way.”

CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a rare, unannounced trip to Moscow in late August, marking the first known visit by a senior Trump administration official to the Russian capital in months. He reportedly warned Russian intelligence officials against attacking NATO territory and pressed Moscow to help reopen the Strait of Hormuz by cutting off Iran.

Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, visited Moscow last week, holding over three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin before flying to Kyiv to brief Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Kushner spoke of Putin’s “aspirations” for Russia, adding that they could be achieved once the war is over — a sign that the U.S. isn’t backing away from its onetime adversary.
Russia US (5050x3367, AR: 1.50)The visits come as Europe deals with aggressive events across the continent that officials say were carried out by Russia, including drones and debris found in Poland, Romania and Germany. The most high-profile incident was a failed explosive drone attack on Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport, a hub for Ukrainian and NATO military logistics, that was attributed to the Kremlin. Experts said the events were a test from Russia to see how NATO allies could and would respond.

But Trump’s posture has been much more relaxed than his own officials’. He told reporters he wasn't worried about a Russian attack on NATO territory, pointing to his own relationship with Putin as reassurance. Asked directly whether his CIA director had warned Russian officials, Trump declined to answer.

And European officials have made attempts to listen to Trump’s grievances publicly. Just in July, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte told Trump, “I know you are disappointed” on Iran.

Despite decades of reliance on American military operations and intelligence, one former State Department official says NATO countries must shift their posture to one in which they depend solely on themselves. Jeff Rathke, who now serves as president of the American-German Institute in Washington, said there’s a growing sense among NATO allies that the alliance cannot depend on U.S. coordination before taking action.

“It has been the Russian foreign policy objective for 25 years to weaken NATO,” Rathke told The Washington Sun. “That has been a Russian aspiration since the time when Vladimir Putin came to power, and the United States’ actions now bring that closer to reality.”

As the incidents attributed to Russia pile up, the question becomes whether NATO should respond. Marta Prochwicz, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations and the deputy head of the organization's Warsaw office, explained that NATO hasn’t really defined how to respond to attacks from Russia outside a full-blown war.

“NATO is not created for that. It's a collective security, but we don't have an answer to this sort of activity. And this is what Russia is exploiting,” she told The Sun.

Prochwicz explained that America’s European allies have begun figuring out how to move along without the U.S.

“There's the sense that you need to be prepared for a contingency where the U.S. basically isn't there,” she told The Sun. “We're not going to prepare defense plans because you can't plan for a military operation without the U.S. That's … out of the question because that's not how NATO was built, and NATO still functions in the old way.”

“But in the hallways, you can start thinking about it,” she added, noting that those familiar with NATO have said the alliance is “like a cat that always falls on its feet.”
Mark Rutte,Donald Trump (8482x5655, AR: 1.50)Those allies are seeing U.S. reticence in action. Trump suggested in an interview with a British broadcaster last week that the U.S. may not back the United Kingdom if Argentina seeks to reestablish control over the Falkland Islands. Trump said he’s reconsidering that support because Britain did not assist the U.S. with the Iran War.

Trump is mistaken, Rathke said, and being part of the alliance does not mean NATO countries must help the United States with all of its interests.

“It was not a treaty obligation for American allies to support every military action the United States took,” Rathke said. “NATO members did not participate in the war in Vietnam.”

But Prochwicz was optimistic this posture won’t last forever.

“A lot of voices in Europe are saying, ‘Let's just move away from the U.S. entirely. Let's lock the door. Let's think of our own stuff. Let's not think about NATO. Let's build a European alternative and just cut ties with the U.S,’” she said. “I think that transatlantic relations are here to stay, and we're just basically having a bad moment.”

entries.title: New Bill Would Limit the Number of Flights Into DCA
entries.summary: Virginia Sens. Tim Kaine and Mark Warner are set to introduce legislation next week that would cap the number of hourly arrivals.
entries.content:
Virginia’s senators want to restrict the number of flights at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport to increase safety after a fatal in-air collision last year.

Democratic Sens. Tim Kaine and Mark Warner are set to introduce legislation next week that would limit the number of hourly arrivals at DCA, according to The Washington Post. The effort comes after an Army helicopter collided with a commercial plane over the Potomac River in January 2025, killing 67 people.

Prior to the 2025 crash, the airport allowed 36 arrivals each hour. That was reduced to 26 following the accident, then gradually increased to the current cadence of 30 per hour. The new bill would decrease hourly arrivals to 28, according to the Post report.

Congress members have long tried to increase the number of flights to and from DCA to make traveling home easier for them, as the Arlington, Virginia, airport is less than a 30-minute drive from the Capitol. Kaine said in an interview with the Post that lawmakers’ travel needs shouldn’t take precedence over general safety.

“The convenience of 535 members of Congress can’t outweigh the safety of 25 million people who use that airport,” Kaine told the Post.

entries.title: Kimmel Says His Interview With James Talarico Won’t Air Due to FCC Pressure
entries.summary: Kimmel said he would instead upload the segment on YouTube.
entries.content:
An interview that Jimmy Kimmel conducted with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico will not air on television amid an ongoing legal dispute between ABC and the Federal Communications Commission, the late-night talk show host said during a Wednesday monologue.

ABC and its parent company Disney sued the FCC on Aug. 18 over accusations that it was threatening broadcast licenses in violation of the First Amendment. The complaint, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., alleged the FCC had “waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts.”

Kimmel said due to ongoing threats from the FCC against himself, his show and ABC, he would instead upload his interview with Talarico on YouTube.

“And thank goodness we have that,” Kimmel said, “because in the America we live in right now, that is the best that we can do until November, of course.”

The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Kimmel and President Donald Trump have shared a contentious relationship stretching back to Trump’s first campaign for office. Since Trump’s return to the presidency last year, the FCC and its chair Brendan Carr have waged a pressure campaign against ABC and Disney that centers around the company’s broadcast licenses.

After the FCC moved to review the broadcast licenses of the network’s owned and operated television stations — years before they were set to expire — ABC accused the commission in a regulatory filing of “retaliating against ABC for the exercise of its First Amendment rights.”

Top Trump administration officials have also targeted the network over its workplace diversity practices, Talarico’s appearance on daytime talk show “The View,” and for remarks Kimmel made in September 2025 after conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s death, which resulted in a brief suspension of his show.

In April, Trump again called on ABC to fire Kimmel after he joked that first lady Melania Trump had the “glow of an expectant widow.” Both Trumps said the remark was a call to violence before the shooting at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner, while Kimmel defended the remark as a reference to the age gap in their relationship.

“I agree that hateful and violent rhetoric is something we should reject,” Kimmel said on his show in April following the criticism. “I think a great place to start to dial that back is having a conversation with your husband about it."

entries.title: Federal Judge Greenlights Contempt Hearing Against Missouri’s GOP Secretary of State
entries.summary: The state Supreme Court has ordered Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to appear for a contempt hearing Thursday for defying its orders.
entries.content:
By David A. Lieb

JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — A federal judge has allowed Missouri’s top court to proceed with a contempt hearing Thursday against Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in a tense and twisting legal battle over whether new congressional districts supported by President Donald Trump can be used in the November election.

Missouri’s battle over its congressional districts has spanned more than a year and spawned confusion over which districts will be in place for voters.

The state’s top court previously ordered Hoskins not to use a Trump-backed map in the general election and instead use districts passed after the last census. But U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark on Tuesday barred Hoskins from using anything other than the new map Trump supports.

The state Supreme Court then ordered Hoskins to appear for a contempt hearing Thursday for not following its orders and instructing local election authorities to use the Trump-backed districts.

State attorneys representing Hoskins had asked Clark to halt the contempt hearing. But Clark declined to do so.

The contempt hearing for Hoskins is scheduled to occur as the U.S. Supreme Court simultaneously considers a request from redistricting opponents to halt Clark's order favoring the Trump-backed congressional map.

Missouri was the second Republican-led state, after Texas, to enact new districts after Trump urged Republicans last year to redraw House districts to their advantage ahead of the midterm elections.

The revised Missouri districts target a Kansas City-based seat held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver by shedding parts into neighboring districts and stretching the remainder into rural Republican areas. The goal is to help Republicans win seven of the state’s eight House seats in the midterm elections — a gain of one seat.

Redistricting opponents collected hundreds of thousands of petition signatures seeking to force a statewide vote on the new districts. They submitted the signatures in December. But Hoskins waited until August — on the same day as Missouri’s primary — to reject the petition. Hoskins asserted that a referendum petition could not be used for congressional redistricting.

The delay allowed Missouri to use the new districts in its August primary. Republican state officials have argued it would violate voters' federal rights to switch districts before the general election.

But the Missouri Supreme Court last week ordered Hoskins to put the redistricting referendum on the November ballot, which he did. It also ruled that the new districts never became law and instead were suspended retroactively to the December petition submission.

The court barred Hoskins from using the new map and said the old map — passed by Republican lawmakers in 2022 after the last census — must be used in the November election. The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to hear an appeal of that decision. But Clark issued his conflicting order moments later.

entries.title: Key Republicans Were Blindsided by Trump’s Call for $5,000 Checks
entries.summary: One senior Senate Republican aide said “it’s not going to happen,” pointing to inflation.
entries.content:
Key congressional Republicans were blindsided by President Donald Trump’s pledge to send $5,000 stimulus checks to American households if the party wins the midterm elections, according to more than a dozen lawmakers, aides and policy experts.

At a midterm rally held in Dallas Wednesday, Trump announced that Congress would approve a dividend payment of $5,000 to “every” adult citizen should Republicans keep the House and Senate in November. The president has made at least two other similar promises during his second administration, none of which have been implemented.

The $1.2 trillion proposal came as a surprise to senior Republicans across Washington, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who had not been briefed on the idea by the White House or consulted ahead of the announcement, the sources told The Washington Sun.

The White House also did not appear to consult with leading conservative think tanks or advocacy groups, they said.

One person briefed on Trump’s pledge described the planning that went into the proposal as “not very vigorous.” The people spoke on the condition of anonymity to talk candidly about private discussions.

The White House has been looking for a way to reverse its declining approval ratings on the economy, which has been plagued by high gas prices and persistent inflation. Trump has long seen the political upside in calling for direct benefit payments to Americans, but congressional Republicans have traditionally opposed the concept as expensive and wasteful.

“Of course they didn’t know. No one knew it was coming. The Republicans on the Hill I talk to were not kept in the loop on this,” said Douglas Holtz-Eakin, the president of the American Action Forum and former director of the Congressional Budget Office. “It’s a bad idea. There’s no need for it economically and it looks desperate politically.”

Several Republican lawmakers have embraced the idea since Trump’s speech. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said in a social media post that he "will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election."

Vice President JD Vance also defended Trump’s proposal as a "dividend for American workers," adding it was a way to help Americans "share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we're creating in the United States."

Still, the consensus on Capitol Hill was that Trump’s proposal was a last-minute political ploy with no chance of advancing even if Republicans do keep both branches of Congress.

One senior Senate Republican aide said “it’s not going to happen” and pointed to the inflation attributed to the stimulus checks approved by the Biden administration during the pandemic.

Republicans are also concerned about the plan’s impact on the deficit. Sending every American a $5,000 dividend would cost roughly $1.2 trillion in a single year, amounting to 3.5% of the nation’s gross domestic product, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan think tank.

Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) criticized the plan on social media, arguing "dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms." Roy told The Washington Sun he had no advance notice on the plan.

Only one GOP lawmaker said he had talked to Trump about the idea. Another person in touch with several Republican congressional offices said, “If there was a heads-up, the circle was very small.”

Rep. Tom Emmer (R-Minnesota), the House majority whip, pointed out that Trump talked about sending dividend payments for the first year of his second term. “Donald Trump thinks out of the box. He's not a traditional policy making legislator,” Emmer said. “And what I found so refreshing last night, while I had never heard the specific number, he wants every American to share in the success.”

Even some of the president’s allies criticized the plan. Stephen Moore, an outside adviser to Trump, agreed that the plan was likely to increase inflation and called on Trump to run on higher take-home pay from faster growth as the result of tax cuts and business deregulation.

“I think it’s not a very good idea,” Moore said. “I’d prefer the Republican plan B: ‘We’ll do more pro-growth thing and we’ll put more money in your pockets.’”

Trump has promised Americans a dividend, rebate, or check 15 times since returning to office, and none of them have materialized, according to a tally by Groundwork Collaborative, a left-leaning organization. The White House announced Thursday that roughly 1 million Americans would be getting $500 rebates starting in “a few weeks” to offset excessive Affordable Care Act fees.

“American voters can add their $5,000 checks to the growing list of empty promises from the president, right below lower prices and a cap on credit card interest rates,” said Elizabeth Pancotti, the organization's vice president for policy, advocacy and research.

Wilbur Ross, who served as commerce secretary during Trump's first term and is attending the convention in Texas, said it’s possible that Republicans will eventually come around to the idea, but it was too soon to say how the party would react. "It was news to everybody," Ross said.

entries.title: Swing and a Miss: Ramaswamy Deletes Viral Batting Cage Video
entries.summary: The clip became an online punch line after an eyewitness raised questions about how the footage was edited.
entries.content:
Vivek Ramaswamy deleted a campaign video of himself taking swings in a batting cage after the clip became an online punch line and an eyewitness raised questions about how the footage was edited.

The Ohio Republican gubernatorial nominee posted the video Tuesday as part of a series outlining “10 things” he would do as governor. Between policy pitches, the video showed Ramaswamy taking swings from an automatic pitching machine.

The footage quickly drew criticism from Democrats and others who mocked Ramaswamy’s form.

David Pepper, the Ohio Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor running alongside gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, used the video to take a broader shot at Ramaswamy’s business career.

“If you think Vivek’s baseball swing is atrocious, wait til you see the disturbing way he first made his millions,” Pepper wrote on X.

The Ohio Democratic Party also took the opportunity to mock Ramaswamy, posting a press release titled “Swing and a Miss! Ten Ways Vivek Ramaswamy Would Strike Out for Ohio’s Working Families.”
https://x.com/KFILE/status/2097703077469921678?s=20Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pennsylvania) also piled on, writing on Facebook that unless something is done about Ramaswamy’s “private equity friends” driving up the cost of youth sports, “American kids will grow up thinking that’s how you hit a baseball.” He accompanied the post with a video of himself in a batting cage.

Ryan Busse, a former Democratic congressional candidate in Montana, mocked Ramaswamy’s swing as particularly at odds with the Republican Party’s emphasis on masculinity.

“The party of ultimate masculinity highlights a gov candidate swinging a bat with the force and form of an 87yr old grandmother,” Busse posted on X.

But the criticism went beyond jokes about Ramaswamy’s swing.

Michael Peacock, who said he was at the same batting cage when Ramaswamy filmed the video, told TiffinOhio.net that Ramaswamy took roughly 25 pitches and made contact only a handful of times. Peacock also said the campaign appeared to reuse footage from the same few swings.

The campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The original video is no longer available on Ramaswamy’s social media accounts, though copies and screenshots continue to circulate online.

Ramaswamy will face Acton in the general election Nov. 3. Recent polling shows the two neck and neck in the race.

entries.title: Appeals Court Compares ICE Detention to Japanese Internment in Scathing Ruling
entries.summary: The Trump administration’s policy of holding undocumented immigrants without bond faced its ninth appeals court loss on Thursday.
entries.content:
A federal appeals court compared the Trump administration’s no-bond immigrant detention policy to the mass internment of Japanese Americans during World War II, in a scathing decision on Thursday.

In the 2-1 ruling, 4th Circuit Court of Appeals Judge Nicole Berner argued that the administration had asked the court to “interpret certain amendments” made to federal immigration laws in 1996 in order to eliminate bond hearings for individuals in Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention.

“Mass detention of marginalized individuals without due process harkens back to some of the darkest moments in our country’s history,” Berner wrote, comparing the ICE detentions to the unconstitutional detainment of Chinese immigrants in the 1890s and the internment of thousands of Japanese people in camps in the 1940s.

Prior to Trump’s interpretation of the federal immigration law, noncitizens were generally released from ICE detention on bond “unless one or more of the following circumstances applied: the noncitizen had committed a certain crime, the noncitizen was considered a flight risk, or the noncitizen posed a danger to his community.”

None of the immigrants in ICE detention — more than 65,000 individuals as of July, according to the public data portal TRAC Immigration — are currently allowed bond hearings, after ICE issued internal guidance in July 2025 to move away from the previous legal standard for detainees.

Thursday’s ruling extended other appeals courts’ decisions to block the policy, marking the ninth such loss for the administration.

“Those shameful and abhorrent past detentions were limited in scope in comparison to the mandatory detention that the Government urges us today to find that Congress established thirty years ago in an ambiguously worded statutory provision,” Berner, a Joe Biden appointee, wrote. “We decline to do so.”

Berner described the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown as a “tsunami” and noted that an “overwhelming majority—over five hundred” federal district courts have rejected the government's interpretation of the law.

“Five presidential administrations, including the first Trump Administration, acted in accordance with this interpretation of the statute,” Berner wrote, adding that the previous precedent for allowing immigrants to be released on bond “provides weighty evidence” in support of the petitioners claim that “they should be provided a bond hearing.”

The Trump administration has lost nine of the 11 appeals court rulings on the issue, and the Supreme Court is likely to pick up the case in its next term.

In her dissent, Judge Allison Jones Rushing, a Trump appointee, argued that the Trump administration’s preference for the “rigidity” found in some federal immigration codes versus the “flexibility” found in other statutes deployed by previous administrations does not mean that the government’s current posture on enforcement is inherently illegal.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: China Says a Trade Deal With U.S. Could Come Soon As Xi's Trip Nears
entries.summary: Weeks before the Chinese president comes to Washington, a Chinese government spokesperson said the countries aim to ax $30 billion of tariffs from each side.
entries.content:
BEIJING — China and the United States hope to reach an agreement on lowering import taxes soon, a Chinese government spokesperson said Thursday, fueling expectations that an announcement could come when the leaders of the two countries meet in two weeks.

Negotiators are striving to implement reciprocal tariff reductions on $30 billion worth of goods “at an early date,” Commerce Ministry spokesperson Huang Ling said at a weekly briefing.

The $30 billion will be from each side, China's official Xinhua News Agency said.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to meet in Washington on Sept. 24 for what will be their third face-to-face talks in the past year. Both governments characterize the meetings as a way to stabilize relations in an era of competing interests between the world's two largest economies.

“Leaders’ diplomacy plays an irreplaceable strategic guiding role in China-U. S. relations,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Thursday.

Trump and Xi agreed at their previous meeting in May in Beijing to launch a U.S.-China Board of Trade that would manage trade between the two countries, along with a parallel Board of Investment. The agreements came after a truce was reached in a blistering tariff war in which Trump hiked tariffs on Chinese imports to extremely high levels and China responded in kind.

The talks on reciprocal tariff reductions are a central part of the negotiations on creating the Board of Trade. The goal is to identify and reduce tariffs on equivalent amounts of “nonsensitive” goods on each side, the U.S. said.

“Trade will be front and center at the summit,” Barclays Bank said in a research note this week on the upcoming Trump-Xi meeting, noting that the truce the two countries reached on tariffs expires on Nov. 10. But it cautioned that the scope for a broad trade deal is limited, and that targeted tariff reductions are more likely.

But as the U.S. and China have already reduced mutual trade reliance, the “overall trade significance will be more limited than before, given the smaller bilateral volume,” said Gary Ng, a senior economist at French bank Natixis.

Chinese exports to the U.S., for example, fell sharply last year, after the U.S. rolled out elevated tariffs.

An agreement on reciprocal tariff reductions could likely benefit the U.S. more, as $30 billion is roughly 28% of its exports to China, while it is only around 10% the other way around, Ng said.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: White House Says It Will Send $500 ACA Rebates to Offset Premium Spikes
entries.summary: Officials have been considering the idea for at least a year, worried voters will punish them for high health insurance costs.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced that about 1 million Americans will receive $500 from the government as a rebate for excessive Affordable Care Act fees.

“Our administration is doing the right thing and giving the money back to the people who were wrongly ripped off,” Trump said in a video posted to X from the White House's account.

Trump said the rebate checks would go out “in just a few weeks.”

The administration said it would send the $500 checks to adults in 30 states, including multiple political battlegrounds with key races to be decided in November: Alaska, New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. The 30 states all rely on the federal marketplace Healthcare.gov, instead of running their own marketplaces.

The effort comes ahead of a second year of double-digit premium spikes on the marketplaces where Americans without employer-sponsored coverage can buy federally subsidized health plans.

Democrats, who passed the 2010 health care law creating the marketplaces, have faced criticism for costly marketplace plans.

But the script flipped last year after congressional Republicans refused to extend pandemic-era subsidies, prompting about 3 million people to leave the marketplaces as their costs rose again. Many middle-income people were no longer eligible for subsidies, leaving them struggling to afford their full monthly premiums.

Marketplace insurers in all 50 states are proposing to hike premiums a median of 15% next year, according to an analysis by KFF, a nonpartisan health policy organization.

Administration officials had floated the idea of rebates in fall 2025, according to sources inside the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Axios first reported the plan on Wednesday.

It's the second refund initiative Trump has announced within 24 hours. Speaking at the GOP midterm convention on Wednesday, Trump promised he would send a $5,000 dividend to every American adult if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The proposal would cost roughly $1.35 trillion and would require congressional approval.

Trump also lauded a one-time dividend of $1,776 sent to military service members last December. The president has proposed other ideas to send money from the federal government to American citizens from savings the administration says came from efforts by the Department of Government Efficiency and tariff refunds. Neither materialized.

He also issued stimulus checks during his first administration to combat a sluggish economy beset by the COVID-19 pandemic.

In his rebate announcement, Trump again pitched his health care plan — a scant, one-page proposal released earlier this year that suggests a few ways to cut costs in the nation’s health care system but falls far short of any kind of comprehensive reform.

entries.title: Supreme Court Blocks Missouri’s Redrawn GOP-Friendly Congressional Map
entries.summary: The decision clears the way for an election with districts used in 2022 instead of a new map that targeted a Democratic-held seat.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court on Thursday stopped Republicans from using new congressional districts state lawmakers had drawn for the midterm election that targeted one of two Democratic U.S. House seats.

The one-page order, which did not include a reason for the decision and had no noted dissents, resolved what had been conflicting rulings between two separate state and federal courts on which map the state should use. The Missouri Supreme Court in one case had ordered state officials to use a map from 2022, and in a separate case a federal district judge later ordered state officials to use the redrawn map.

The Supreme Court blocked the order by the federal district judge. Previously, the Supreme Court had declined a request from state officials to halt the decision by the state Supreme Court, which had ruled the state should use the 2022 congressional maps and put a referendum on the redistricted maps ahead of voters in November.

"Missourians don't need a Secretary of State who manufactures confusion; they need one who follows the law,” Richard von Glahn, the executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, wrote in a statement shortly following the U.S. Supreme Court ruling. “Denny Hoskins has had every chance to do that and chose not to. The courts have settled this, now it's up to Missouri voters to finish the job,” referring to the referendum vote that now appears set to take place in November.

The Supreme Court order came less than an hour before Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins was set to appear before the state Supreme Court over potential contempt charges. In court on Thursday morning, lawyers for Hoskins said that the secretary was “aware” of the Supreme Court ruling, and that he would be “looking to implement this court's injunction.”

“How that technically happens, that’s what’s being evaluated right now,” the attorney said, while noting that there could be “more litigation to be done should the plaintiffs choose to do that.”

Missouri officials and the Trump administration filed briefs in the case in support of using the Republican maps and opposing the request for a stay, just minutes before the Supreme Court ruled.

The state and Trump administration argued that such a decision would “disenfranchise hundreds of thousands of Missourians who voted in the Primary,” which was held under the redistricted maps.

Missouri was one of the first states to redraw its map last summer after President Donald Trump called on Republican state lawmakers to redistrict to their advantage. The redrawn map, which was ushered through both chambers in the state legislature last September, split Kansas City three ways in an effort to draw out Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s seat.

Per Missouri law, voters can challenge state law through petitions. People Not Politicians gathered more than twice the number of necessary signatures to force a referendum by the end of 2025. In August, Hoskins refused to certify the signatures, setting off the series of legal challenges.
entries.author: Manuela Silva

entries.title: Maryland Utility Joins Lawsuit Over Potomac River Spill
entries.summary: The Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission says the drinking water for 1 million residents is near rundown sections of a sewage line.
entries.content:
Sections of a massive sewage line that burst in January, spilling 243 million gallons of untreated waste into the Potomac River, are in equally bad or worse shape than the part that collapsed, according to a new court filing in a lawsuit against DC Water.

One of those sections of the pipeline, called the Potomac Interceptor, is near the drinking water supply for 1 million Maryland residents, the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission said in a court filing Wednesday asking to join a Justice Department lawsuit against the local water authority. A judge approved the request Thursday.

DC Water began emergency repair work in June on the section near WSSC Water’s drinking supply and is expected to complete the work by the end of this month. Still, the remaining weak areas of the pipes pose a threat of further disruption, the memorandum said.

The federal lawsuit seeks financial penalties from DC Water, which the Justice Department said failed to properly operate and maintain the sewer system leading to the leak. WSSC Water, in a proposed complaint, also wants a judge to order DC Water to repair all segments of the pipeline that are “in condition equal to or worse than the segment that collapsed,” among other demands.

The Interceptor is a 54-mile sewer line carrying 60 million gallons of sewage daily. It was constructed in the 1960s and broke after years of poor maintenance, leading to dangerous E. coli levels and shutting down fish harvesting for almost two months. DC Water had known about the deterioration for at least seven years before the pipe failed.

WSSC Water says the disruption of the Interceptor impeded its ability to treat wastewater and that another burst pipe would risk contaminating drinking water supply.

The agency also pointed to the fiscal impact of the repairs, which it said DC Water estimated will cost $59.3 million. DC Water allocated 30.9% of that cost to WSSC Water and none to itself, WSSC Water’s complaint said. It is unclear which other agencies may have been assigned to pick up the tab by DC Water.

entries.title: Kamala Harris Plots Midterm Campaign Trail Blitz
entries.summary: The appearances come as several Democratic candidates have sought to distance themselves from the former vice president.
entries.content:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris will appear at events to boost Sen. Jon Ossoff’s reelection bid in the coming weeks, a campaign spokesperson for the Georgia Democrat confirmed to The Washington Sun Thursday.

The campaign trail appearance is reportedly one of several that Harris has planned ahead of November’s midterms. Her appearance also comes as some Democratic candidates and strategists have signaled they are distancing themselves from the 2024 presidential nominee, who has maintained a relatively low profile since her departure from the White House.

Harris is expected to deliver a keynote address at a Fulton County Democrats dinner and stump with Ossoff in October, CNN first reported Thursday. She has also previously appeared in social media videos for Ossoff’s campaign.

“Senator Ossoff is grateful for Vice President Harris' help and support in his re-election campaign,” Ossoff campaign spokesperson Ellie Dougherty said in a statement Thursday.

Harris is also scheduled to be a featured guest at a fundraising event in San Diego for Marni von Wilpert, who is running for California's 48th Congressional District, according to Politico. She will also appear in Northern California to stump for Richard Pan, whose opponent is independent Rep. Kevin Kiley in the state’s newly redrawn 6th Congressional District.

Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, who is running for governor, told Politico that Harris is planning to attend a canvass launch for his campaign in October.

Harris’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on her upcoming appearances.

“It is critical for Democrats to win this November so we can fight the Trump administration’s corruption and work to lower costs for the American people,” her spokesperson Eduardo Negrón told CNN. “Vice President Harris will continue to do whatever is needed to support candidates in races where she can be helpful.”

Negrón previously said that Harris intends to fundraise and make appearances for races “where she can help make a difference.”

Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek, Iowa gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand and Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola are among the Democrats who have held Harris at arm’s length after her underperformance in 2024 led to a reckoning within the Democratic Party.

“No thanks,” Sand told reporters late August when questioned about his stance. “Let’s move on. We need some new leadership.”

entries.title: Hitting Coaches Break Down Vivek Ramaswamy’s Baseball Swing
entries.summary: The candidate for Republican governor was mocked for his swing in a campaign video. We asked experts to weigh in.
entries.content:
Look, it’s not easy to hit a baseball. But after Vivek Ramaswamy posted a video of himself in a batting cage this week, interspersing swings with some of his key campaign talking points, the internet did not spare the Republican candidate for Ohio governor.

In the interest of fairness, I sought some expert opinions, asking a handful of professional hitting coaches to break down the tape.

First, a college head coach who specializes in hitting looked at Ramaswamy’s mechanics. The video, posted to Ramaswamy’s official Instagram account, includes him taking 11 cuts in khaki pants, polo shirt tucked in. In between those shots, he laid out 10 things he would do for Ohio if he were elected governor.

“Front foot hitter with horizontal path,” the college coach said in a text. “Most hitting coaches would coach that out of him but it works for him and could make it serviceable.”

“He has a shot??” I asked. I am still not sure what I meant by shot, in this case, but it just felt like the right follow-up question.

“Not a shot in hell,” the coach responded. “Maybe at the batting cage only lol.”

Ramaswamy is running against Democrat Amy Acton. It’s not the first time Ramaswamy, formerly of the Department of Government Efficiency (or DOGE), has used sports in campaign videos. It is common for politicians to tap into sports, especially in an effort to appear more relatable to the average voter. Sometimes that feels natural, like when New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani talks about his Arsenal fandom. And other times it can flop, like back in May when New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she would challenge President Donald Trump to name the starting lineup of the Knicks’ title-winning team in 1993. (That year, the Chicago Bulls beat the Phoenix Suns in the NBA Finals.)

What is less common, though, is politicians actually playing when trying to use sports for political gain. Ramaswamy’s first attempt at this was much more natural. Like the baseball clip, he started the video by saying: “Here’s 10 things I’m gonna do for Ohio.” But instead of a batting cage, he was on a tennis court, where he’s clearly spent a lot of time. That video is pinned to the top of Ramaswamy’s Instagram account. The baseball video is no longer on his main grid, as it was Wednesday, though it still exists if you click over to his reels.

Here, then, is further evidence that a great tennis swing doesn’t translate to baseball (or vice versa). Ramaswamy’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment Thursday.

“Oh man, where to even start?” a California-based hitting guru said when I asked about Ramaswamy’s cage session. “Very, very, very much a front-foot hitter, so that's the first thing we'd attack. But I'm not sure it's salvageable. Looks like a lot of groundballs right back to the pitcher. Needs a much better swing path to get the ball in the air. Stick to ... politics?”

A prominent hitting coach from the Dominican Republic went tongue-in-cheek with his response. “Nice swing, good balance, tremendous finish,” he said in a text. “Executed a perfect contact point, comparable to Manny Ramirez! 600 million on the open market!” Some of Ramaswamy’s political opponents, however, were not feeling as silly about it.

Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pennsylvania) wrote on X: “Congrats to Vivek, who today apparently swung a baseball bat for the first time in his life.” And Rep. Chris Deluzio’s (D-Pennsylvania) team cut a video that showed his swing right after Ramaswamy’s, including a highlight of Deluzio hitting a ball to the warning track in a past Congressional Baseball Game.

Deluzio’s X post said: “If we don’t do something about [Vivek Ramaswamy]’s private equity friends jacking up the cost of youth sports, American kids will grow up thinking that’s how you hit a baseball.” Deluzio then used his video to promote the Let Kids Play Act, a bill he introduced, along with Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), that would ban private equity companies from investing in youth sports.

entries.title: Trump Admin Sues to End In-State Tuition for Undocumented Immigrants in D.C.
entries.summary: The District has become the latest battleground for the push to end in-state tuition benefits for undocumented immigrants.
entries.content:
D.C. has become the latest battleground for the Trump administration's push to end in-state tuition benefits for undocumented immigrants.

The Justice Department filed a complaint in federal court Thursday seeking to overturn D.C.’s policy offering in-state tuition rates to undocumented immigrants, calling it unconstitutional and discriminatory against students from other states.

“This rule constitutes blatant unequal treatment favoring illegal aliens over U.S. citizens. Worse, such preferential treatment is squarely prohibited and preempted by Congress,” the lawsuit said.

The Trump administration had filed 21 similar lawsuits in other states as of Aug. 27 with varying degrees of success. A federal judge ended Kansas’ policy allowing in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants Wednesday. Other states such as Oklahoma and Nebraska chose to stop their policies. Minnesota successfully won its case earlier this year, but the Justice Department appealed the decision.

The Justice Department and University of the District of Columbia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The Mayor's office referred questions to the D.C. Attorney General, who did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

entries.title: Trump Administration Awards $45 Million Contract for New Air Force One Simulator
entries.summary: The flight simulator for the Qatari-gifted plane is publicly funded and may not be ready for “24-36 months.”
entries.content:
The Trump administration on Wednesday awarded a $45.3 million contract to construct a flight simulator to train pilots and aircrew to fly his new Air Force One, a luxury Boeing 747-8 that was gifted to the United States by Qatar.

The sole-source contract between the Presidential and Executive Airpower Directorate and Florida-based CAE USA Inc. directs the company to install a “commercial FAA Level D certified 747-8i Full Flight Simulator” — the model of aircraft President Donald Trump accepted as a gift from the Qatari royal family — at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.

Trump has long maintained that the gifted plane, estimated to be worth $400 million, came at no cost to taxpayers and that he would be “stupid” not to accept it. The flight simulator contract, however, demonstrates that there are taxpayer-funded costs associated with the new jumbo jet.

The contract also raises questions about the timeline for the Qatari-gifted plane. Trump has floated the idea of taking it with him after his presidency to showcase in his Florida presidential library. But the flight simulator specialized for the plane may take years to be ready, per the details of the contract.

The installation is expected to take “24-36 months from contract award,” with future support and maintenance estimated to last “12-18 months,” per the project description. That period “will also include the courseware and flight instruction to train pilots, instructors, and aircrew personnel.”

The simulator could get use, too, for a pair of future Air Force One 747-8 replacement planes that have been delayed for years, as well as an already-delivered 747-8 training aircraft.

CAE USA is a major contractor with the Department of Defense, having delivered flight simulators for other military aircraft, including B2 bombers and F-16 fighters. The company has manufactured “all of the commercial Level D certified 747-8 simulators worldwide,” according to an Air Force “Justification and Approval” document.

“The 747-8i FFS is vital for conducting initial pilot qualification, recurrent proficiency, as well as other aircrew training exercises,” the contract document reads.

The simulator is expected to have “full motion system with aerodynamic modeling and performance data, visual system, sound system, cockpit environment, aircraft systems simulation,” as well as “realistic aircraft movement and G-forces.”

The White House deferred questions about the contract and the future of the new Air Force One plane to the Department of Defense, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In July, Trump opted not to use either the new or old Boeing 747 normally used as Air Force One to fly back from Turkey. Instead, he flew out on a different, smaller government plane after sneaking out of the old Air Force One in a catering truck.

That same month, the Department of Justice issued, then retracted, subpoenas to New York Times reporters who had reported on security concerns surrounding the new Air Force One.

Trump’s trip Wednesday to a Republican convention in Dallas was delayed after one of the emergency slides on the new Air Force One plane was accidentally deployed.
