entries.title: New Mexico Lawmakers Urge Apple, Google to Publicly Reject Trump’s ‘New America’ Name
entries.summary: Trump has not issued an executive order mandating the name change, but Democratic lawmakers want to head off any potential future revisions.
entries.content:
New Mexico lawmakers are calling on Apple and Google to keep using New Mexico on their map applications rather than President Donald Trump’s suggested name for the state, “New America.”

Unlike other name changes Trump made through executive orders, the president has only floated New Mexico’s name change in social media posts and public comments — but the coalition of New Mexico Democrats are taking what they call Trump’s “threatening” posts seriously.

In a letter sent Thursday, Democratic Sens. Ben Ray Luján and Martin Heinrich and Reps. Teresa Leger Fernández, Melanie Stansbury and Gabe Vasquez urged the tech companies to “publicly commit” to keeping their state’s name unchanged by Sept. 18.

The group’s letter to Apple CEO John Ternus and Google CEO Sundar Pichai beseeched the executives to reject Trump's recommendation “regardless of what the President posts on social media, what executive order he attempts to issue, or what pressure he puts on your companies.”

“Let us be clear: the President has no legal authority to rename New Mexico. Our state’s name belongs to the people of New Mexico and is rooted in our history and our Constitution, which clearly states that ‘the name of this state is New Mexico,’” the lawmakers wrote.

Apple and Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Washington Sun.

After Trump posted a series of maps featuring the border state with the name “New America” on Truth Social over the weekend, the president doubled down on the idea in his remarks at the first day of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

“You have a neighboring state, New Mexico. We think it should be called New America,” Trump told the crowd on Wednesday. “I’ll tell you, the people love the idea.”

When asked if Trump had contacted either company regarding the name change, the White House referred The Sun to his convention comments.

Trump’s comments and posts about renaming New Mexico come amid his continued efforts to retitle other landmarks and bodies of water to reflect what the White House deems “names that honor American greatness.”

Apple and Google have changed the names to reflect Trump’s titles for the Gulf of Mexico to be the “Gulf of America,” Alaska’s Mount Denali to “Mount McKinley” and most recently Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

In each of those cases, the president issued an executive order requiring the name changes — in contrast to his mere statements and posts floating New Mexico’s potential new name. Trump reportedly pressured Apple to change the name to “Lake America,” and the company quickly acquiesced.

Apple and Google both serve substantial international audiences, and some companies have pushed back on the president’s name changes citing a similar customer base.

The Associated Press adopted the “Mount McKinley” name since it is located within the U.S., but the publication — which publishes a dominant style guide for journalists — rejected Trump’s push to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario because the bodies of water share a border with Mexico and Canada, respectively.

The U.S. has a contentious trade relationship with Mexico and is currently in an all-out trade war with Canada.

New York, New Jersey and New Hampshire also have names referencing a place outside of the U.S. — named after an English leader, county and island off the coast of the country, respectively.

Only New Mexico has received the recent influx of scrutiny from the president.

entries.title: DOJ Directs States to Preserve 2024 Election Records As It Seeks Their Voter Data
entries.summary: The department warned election officials that failure to comply could prompt "civil and criminal sanctions."
entries.content:
By Josh Kelety, Alanna Durkin Richer and Gary Fields

The Trump administration is ordering officials in more than two dozen states to preserve records from the 2024 election as part of a campaign to force states to turn over detailed voter records despite repeated court losses.

The Justice Department sent letters to 29 states and the District of Columbia instructing election officials not to destroy the records. Those are places the Trump administration has sued in a bid to gain access to voter registration information that contains addresses, dates of birth, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers.

In one letter obtained by The Associated Press, a Justice Department official told Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, a Republican, that she is “under investigation" and subject to ongoing litigation over the state’s failure to turn over statewide voter registration lists. The Justice Department declined to elaborate Thursday on the nature of the investigation.

“The purpose of this letter is to notify you of your obligations to take reasonable steps to conduct a litigation hold and preserve and retain all hard copy documents and electronically stored information,” wrote Eric Neff, acting chief of the Civil Rights Division's Voting Section.

The letter warns election officials that their “failure to preserve relevant data may constitute spoliation of evidence," which could subject them to “civil and criminal sanctions.”

In a social media post Thursday, Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Civil Rights Division, said the Justice Department sent the letters to ensure states do not destroy election records related to the lawsuits that seek to compel election officials to hand over voter registration lists.

“This is standard litigation practice, not a ‘threat,’” Dhillon said in a post on X.

Henderson, Utah's top elections official, said in an interview that her office received the letter Friday.

“No letter — and we’ve gotten a lot of letters from the Department of Justice over the past year — not a single one of them said that we were under investigation for anything,” Henderson said. “It was a little bit alarming at first to see those words.”

Henderson said her office understands the need to hold onto records during litigation.

“What’s not helpful is the constant barrage of attacks and harassment and accusations, baseless accusations, that do nothing to help secure our elections,” she said.

Her office also received a letter from the DOJ in July asserting that election officials could be prosecuted if votes from noncitizens are counted in their vote tallies.

Other election offices, including the secretaries of state for Arizona and Minnesota, confirmed they also received the letter.

“Our office will follow the law,” said Calli Jones, spokesperson for the Arizona office. “Any implication from this letter or others that implies we are not following the law is disrespectful to the work that election administrators do across Arizona and the country.”

Minnesota Secretary of State spokesperson Cassondra Knudson said the office will comply with the Justice Department's request but noted that it goes beyond the federal requirement of maintaining records for 22 months following an election.

Justice Department is in long-running conflict with states over voter data

The preservation demand could set the stage for the Justice Department to seek access to the states' election records as part of the administration’s hunt for fraud. The FBI has already obtained records or election equipment related to either the 2020 or 2024 elections from the most populous counties in the battleground states of Arizona, Georgia and Michigan without saying what it was searching for.

The letters escalate a fight between the Trump administration over access to the sensitive voter information. Federal officials have said they need the voter data to ensure that states are complying with federal election laws related to maintaining voter registration lists, even though states already have detailed processes to do that.

Some election officials have raised concerns that the request conflicts with state privacy laws. They also are concerned that federal officials will use the sensitive data for other purposes, such as searching for potential noncitizens. In one case, a Justice Department attorney acknowledged the department was seeking unredacted voter roll information so it could be shared with the Department of Homeland Security to check citizenship status.

Judges have repeatedly dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuits seeking access to the detailed state voter information, and Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested the administration might take the fight to the U.S. Supreme Court.

The letters come as the administration continues to raise concerns about the potential for voter fraud — in particular, noncitizen voting. While voter fraud and voting by noncitizens does occur, it's rare and gets prosecuted. There has been no evidence of widespread fraud marring American elections.

Trump issued an executive order earlier this year that sought to create a federal voter list and directly involve the U.S. Postal Service in election operations in a way that would limit mail voting. A challenge to that order is now before the Supreme Court. The president also has pushed Congress to pass a bill requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote and have it take effect for the midterms.

entries.title: San Francisco Mayor Declares AI-driven Housing Shortage a ‘Rent Emergency’
entries.summary: “We have lived through booms before,” Daniel Lurie said in an announcement launching his new tenant-focused policy platform.
entries.content:
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie declared a “rent emergency” Thursday, citing a combination of rising rent prices and a meandering housing supply that has pushed city evictions to record numbers.

Lurie’s announcement included a broad policy package aimed at “helping San Franciscans stay in their homes” by delaying evictions and preventing sudden rent spikes.

“Leaders from across government and across the city are standing together, united behind a sweeping package of reforms and investments to provide renters greater stability,” Lurie, a Democrat, said Thursday.

The Levi Strauss heir has unique alliances with Silicon Valley executives, and ran on the promise to bridge gaps with the city’s progressive core, particularly regarding housing. San Francisco is reporting decade-high eviction notices and officials say thousands of residents are behind on rent or are burdened with "shadow debt" borrowed from private lenders to stay housed.

While the city’s rent woes aren’t new, a surge in artificial intelligence-industry jobs has spiked immediate demand for housing.

In his new plan, Lurie proposes six ordinances and $30 million in investments that he says will help protect renters — including a provision to bar evictions for people who owe less than a month’s rent — prevent rent spikes and grant tenants with legal tools to fight unlawful landlord behavior. The package would also allocate $27 million to maintain rental subsidies for low-income households.

The emergency declaration doesn’t allow the mayor’s office to sidestep red tape as a disaster declaration would, but is a symbolic move meant to coalesce city leaders around the new policy proposals

“We have lived through booms before,” Lurie said. “This time, we have an opportunity to build a recovery that is broad-based and lasting, where San Franciscans can put down roots and participate in our city’s success.”

Rents have leaped aggressively across San Francisco in recent years. The average one-bedroom apartment now goes for $4,300 per month, according to city data, and just 2.2% of the city’s multifamily housing is vacant and available for rent as of June 2026 — surpassing New York City, where Mayor Zohran Mamdani implemented aggressive housing reforms this year.

entries.title: Joseph diGenova Ends His Role Overseeing Florida-Based Investigation Into Trump Foes
entries.summary: “It was an honor and a privilege to serve the president and the department,” diGenova said.
entries.content:
Joseph diGenova, the MAGA loyalist who oversaw a Florida-based investigation that was widely perceived to be a personal vengeance mission against President Donald Trump’s political enemies, quit Thursday afternoon.

DiGenova, who was sworn in as counselor to the attorney general in April, sent the Department of Justice a letter at 3 p.m. informing top officials of his decision, he told The Washington Sun.

“It was an honor and a privilege to serve the president and the department,” he said, declining to elaborate on why he stepped down.

Among the many targets of the inquest was former CIA director John Brennan, who was being criminally investigated over his handling of the Obama administration’s probe into Trump-Russia connections that muddied the 2016 presidential election and followed Trump throughout his first term, according to two sources familiar with the investigation.

That grand jury investigation, although cloaked in secrecy, appeared to be a frustrated effort that was briefly pursued in Washington but eventually relocated to South Florida, where top DOJ officials could count on a loyal Trump appointee, U.S. Attorney Jason A. Reding Quiñones, to be in charge of the case.

The investigation was specifically based in Fort Pierce, where the local federal district court keeps a single judge at a faraway outpost: U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, also a Trump appointee regarded by the White House to be politically amenable.

After a relatively quiet period that lasted several months, The Associated Press reported on Tuesday that the DOJ issued a new round subpoenas seeking testimony before a grand jury there — signs that prosecutors were still moving forward on a case that purports to show the existence of an anti-Trump grand conspiracy across U.S. spy agencies.

entries.title: Trump Moves the Medal of Honor Monument Forward While Veering Back Into His Usual Hits
entries.summary: At an event to sign a bill that authorizes a place to commemorate Medal recipients in D.C., Trump talks tariffs, the border and foreign investments.
entries.content:
A monument honoring Medal of Honor recipients is a step closer to fruition after President Donald Trump signed a bill authorizing a new D.C.-based monument Thursday at the National Medal of Honor Museum.

Before the signing, Trump toured the museum in Arlington, Texas — pausing for an apparent economic discussion with Medal recipients in front of an Army helicopter — and gave remarks that touched on the monument. But he quickly turned to his usual stump speech, with tangents on tariffs, the border and the cleanliness of downtown D.C.

“With this museum and a new monument in Washington, D.C., America will never ever forget what they did, and what they risked and how much they’ve risked, what they meant to our families and what they’ve meant to our country,” Trump said.

Named after Heschel “Woody” Williams, the last World War II Medal of Honor recipient, the bill ensures that the monument will have a prominent location on the National Mall. Sixteen recipients attended the signing. Joining them were Rep. Blake Moore (R-Utah) and Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia), who sponsored the bill, with Williams’ family also in attendance.

Trump said during his remarks that the monument was originally to be erected near the Lincoln Memorial, but he indicated that is no longer the case. He paused and said that location was taken, but that the administration would find a better location for the monument.

During his museum tour, Trump stopped to greet seven Medal recipients. After taking a picture with them, Trump could be heard telling the recipients about investments in American industry.

“Twenty trillion dollars this year,” Trump said. “It’s never been anywhere near it.”

One recipient in front of the president responded, “I don’t understand trillions.” Trump patted him on the shoulder and said, “He doesn’t understand money.”

Trump’s speech resembled a shortened version of his Wednesday night address at the GOP midterm convention, including his recent repeated riff on the looks of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for Senate. Trump later joked that he would like to receive a Medal of Honor.

“Tonight, the story will be that Donald Trump wants the Congressional Medal of Honor,” Trump said. “I’m only kidding. Actually, I’m not kidding.”

Describing the monument as the final piece of a project to safeguard and remember recipients, museum Chair Charlotte Jones called the signing a “giant leap forward” toward the monument’s existence.

“I have been asked many times why this project hasn’t already been built and why it doesn’t exist already,” Jones said. “Every time I answer, ‘I think it is because our country needs it now more than ever before.’”

Trump visited the meeting while in town for the GOP midterm convention. He spoke at the convention Wednesday night and was scheduled to address convention attendees again on Thursday night.
entries.author: Ben T.N. Mause

entries.title: DHS Deletes AI Immigration Post After Backlash
entries.summary: The post, which urged a bearded man with a turban to “self-deport,” was part of the department’s messaging campaign against immigrant commercial drivers.
entries.content:
The Department of Homeland Security deleted a social media post featuring a Sikh man and an Optimus Prime-like character after the graphic drew accusations that the Trump administration was using a racial stereotype to promote its immigration crackdown.

The post, which appeared Wednesday on DHS’ official X account, showed the “Transformers” character confronting a bearded man wearing a turban. The AI-generated image included the message “Self-deport or find out” and told “Mr. Singh” — one of the most common surnames among Sikh men — to get off American roads because he did not “know how to drive.”

DHS has launched a broader campaign this year targeting immigrants working as commercial drivers, claiming it wants to tighten enforcement against people who are undocumented or unlicensed. The department has highlighted fatal crashes involving immigrant truck drivers as part of its push and even opened a tip line asking Americans to report any truck driver they suspect of being undocumented.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, DHS said its post depicted Harjinder Singh, an Indian truck driver accused of causing a fatal crash in Florida last year when his 18-wheeler collided with a minivan on the highway, killing three people in the other vehicle. Singh has pleaded not guilty to vehicular homicide and manslaughter charges.

DHS told The Sun that criticism of the post was “nonsensical drivel” and “faux outrage.” The department has said Singh, who obtained a work permit and driver’s license in California, was not in the U.S. legally after he entered the country in 2018.

“Harjinder Singh is an illegal alien from India who should never have been in our country,” the DHS statement said.

The Sikh Coalition said Wednesday’s post amounted to racial profiling and pointed to a long history of Sikhs in the United States, including in the trucking industry. The Hindu American Foundation also condemned the graphic as racist and anti-Indian.

“Millions of Sikhs in the United States have the last name Singh, which means lion. We remain fearless in identifying as Sikhs—even when our government portrays us as enemies,” the Sikh Coalition posted on X.

The department has faced growing criticism over its use of AI-generated imagery and pop-culture references in its immigration messaging.

In a separate post that is still available on the official X profile, the department used AI to create a video that featured Transformer-like creatures targeting several truck drivers officials said were in the country illegally — including Singh, who was dressed similarly to the man depicted in the now-deleted post.

“We will defend ourselves. We will defend Americanism. We will defend our home,” the caption for the video reads.

Hasbro, which owns the Transformers franchise, said in a statement that the administration was using the likeness of its characters without permission.

“Optimus Prime is a beloved character who represents humility, leadership, compassion and justice,” Hasbro said. “These posts were done without permission and do not represent the Transformers brand or Hasbro.”

entries.title: The $1.2 Trillion Surprise
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Afternoon Sun newsletter for Sept. 10, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Key Republicans say they were blindsided by Trump’s call for $5,000 checks, The Sun’s Jeff Stein, Al Weaver and Reese Gorman report.

  • The $1.2 trillion surprise proposal shocked senior Republicans, including John Thune. The White House does not appear to have consulted leading conservative think tanks or advocacy groups, either.
  • JD Vance defended the idea, and Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said he will “get a bill ready” to get the “Trump Dividend” passed immediately after the midterms.
Trump also announced that around 1 million Americans will receive $500 from the government as a rebate for excessive Affordable Care Act fees.

A federal appeals court denied the Trump administration’s request to lift a block on new rules for mail-in ballots before the midterms. The case is awaiting the Supreme Court’s weigh-in.





THE HILL

Sen. Chris Van Hollen sent a letter to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressing concern about the company’s latest model, the Afternoon Sun first reports. The Maryland Democrat is requesting a public response about potential gaps in the company’s safety framework for its GPT-6 Astra model.

New Mexico lawmakers called on Apple and Google to keep using New Mexico on their map applications rather than Trump’s suggested name for the state, New America.





THE ADMINISTRATION

Scoop: The Trump administration awarded a $45.3 million contract to construct a flight simulator to train pilots and aircrew to fly his Qatari-gifted Air Force One, The Sun’s Mark Alfred reports.

A Jimmy Kimmel interview with Texas Democrat James Talarico will not air on television amid an ongoing legal dispute between ABC and the FCC. The segment will be uploaded onto YouTube instead.





THE COURTS

The Supreme Court stopped Missouri Republicans from using their new GOP-friendly congressional map that targeted one of two Democratic U.S. House seats.

  • The Missouri Supreme Court ruled state Secretary of State Denny Hoskins had violated its order by directing officials to use a map the court had already rejected — but said Hoskins had since “purged himself of contempt” by directing officials to not use it about an hour before the court’s 2 p.m. hearing.
Denver and several advocacy groups asked a federal judge to prohibit the Trump administration from deploying federal immigration agents to polling sites ahead of the midterms.

A federal appeals court compared the Trump administration’s no-bond immigrant detention policy to the mass internment of Japanese Americans during World War II, in a scathing decision.





THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL
